summary: `roomForRead` is the only background wait in the plugin that never consults `isStale(generation)` and issues its I/O *before* checking `stopped`, so a blocking `fetchRecent` on an unprovisioned topic keeps talking to the homeserver after `disconnect()` has cleared the token, joins a room post-teardown, and resurrects the `rooms` registry.
failure: Reproduced: `fake.aliasExists=false`, `sync_timeout_ms:300`, then `fetchRecent({topic:'never', since:asCursor(''), blockMs:5000})`; `disconnect()` at 50ms and the alias appears immediately after. Instrumented output: post-disconnect requests `[/directory/room/%23parley_never%3Afake, POST /rooms/!room%3Afake/join, /messages, /messages]`, each with `authorization: null` (token already cleared), `rooms.size` back to 1, and the seam call *resolving with a message* read after teardown. With the shipped default `sync_timeout_ms: 25000` the same call resolves ~25s after disconnect (measured 4032ms at a 4000ms setting). Because the loop exits only on `remaining<=0 || this.stopped`, a `connect()` (which sets `stopped=false` and clears `rooms`) lets the OLD generation's loop resume and write into the NEW generation's room cache.
remediation: Capture `const generation = this.generation` in `fetchRecent`/`roomForRead` and gate the loop on `this.isStale(generation)` — checked *before* the `existingRoom()` call, not only after it — and make the wait interruptible (an AbortController registered in `this.controllers`, or race the delay against a disconnect promise) so teardown is immediate rather than one `sync_timeout_ms` late.
testUpgrade: Widen `reconnect-lifecycle.fake.test.ts`'s LIFECYCLES x REGISTRIES table with a `roomExists: boolean` axis and add a `blocking fetchRecent in flight` lifecycle row: for every (lifecycle, roomExists) cell assert (a) the pending seam call settles within one fake round-trip of the disconnect, (b) zero requests reach the fake after `disconnect()` returns, and (c) all four registries are 0 and stay 0. Guards the CLASS 'a plugin wait that watches only `stopped`', and stays reusable for any future poll-until-provisioned loop.

summary: `FakeSynapse` returns the same `ROOM_ID` for every alias and models exactly one timeline, so the entire fast suite is blind to the topic->room mapping. The whole `shared: false` axis (~40 rows) is decoration, and no test asserts which alias the READ path resolves.
failure: I replaced the plugin's entire topic->room mapping with constants — `roomKey()` always returns `'�shared'` and `roomLocalpart()` always builds `parley_ctx-payments`, so every topic resolves to and provisions one room and all topics share one cache slot. Result: 195 passed / 4 skipped, unchanged. `provisioning.fake.test.ts` does assert `room_alias_name`, but the only topic it ever provisions is literally `ctx-payments`, so it cannot fire. In production (`shared_room` unset — the configuration the README calls production) `belongs()` returns true unconditionally, so this bug would silently cross-deliver every topic into every other topic's catch-up and live path with no second line of defence: a total topic-allowlist bypass that the always-run suite grades as green. The only test that would catch it, `live-per-topic.test.ts`, is `describe.skipIf(!bothAccounts)`.
remediation: Give the fake a real alias directory: mint a distinct `room_id` per alias, key timelines by `room_id`, and 404 `/messages`, `/sync` and `/context` for an unknown room. Then parameterize the existing shared/per-topic tables over TWO topics and assert per-topic isolation (topic A's `fetchRecent` and `subscribe` never see topic B's message) plus the exact alias each read path resolved.
testUpgrade: Add a `room-isolation.fake.test.ts` table over {per-topic, shared_room} x {post, fetchRecent(no since), fetchRecent(since), subscribe} x two topics, asserting (a) in per-topic mode each seam call touches only its own topic's room_id and returns only its own messages, (b) in shared mode both land on the one shared room and are separated by the tag, and (c) the resolved alias string for each topic. Guards the CLASS 'a fake with one instance of the resource the plugin routes over'; the same widened fake also lets `sanitizeAlias` and the alias-length limit be graded.

summary: `drainForward` decides a page is 'full' with `chunk.length >= limit`, but `/context`'s `end` token re-includes the `since` event, so that event consumes a slot. At exactly `limit - 1` trailing foreign events the end-of-timeline page is misjudged as full and the topic's cursor advances on another topic's traffic alone — the precise behaviour the code comment and the test's own CLASS docstring say must not happen.
failure: Reproduced (shared_room, limit 5). Sweeping the foreign-block depth: count=1,2,3 -> cursor stays at `$e0` (correct); count=4 -> cursor MOVES to `$e4`, a topic-B `event_id`, although the timeline ended there; count=5,6 -> moves (correct). So `fetchRecent({topic:A, since:idA0, limit:5})` after `post(A,'a0')` plus exactly 4 posts to topic B returns `{messages: [], nextCursor: <a topic-B event id>}` instead of the stable `idA0`. The `FOREIGN_BLOCKS` table in `catchup-sync.fake.test.ts` uses counts 1,2,10,15 — it straddles the boundary and never lands on it. The conformance suite's `since at the tail returns empty and a stable cursor` is therefore a real (if low-probability) flake for Matrix, which runs in shared_room mode where sibling tests supply the foreign traffic.
remediation: Compute fullness on the post-exclusivity count rather than the raw chunk length: compare the number of events remaining after dropping the re-included `since` event against `limit`, or request `limit + 1` and treat `> limit` as full.
testUpgrade: Replace FOREIGN_BLOCKS' four hand-picked counts with a swept range 0..2*limit (and repeat the sweep at limit 1 and 2), each row asserting `movesTheCursor === (count >= limit)` plus replayability. Guards the CLASS 'a page-fullness test that never lands on limit-1 / limit / limit+1'; apply the same sweep to `recentWindow`'s backward paging.

summary: `backfill`'s `skip` set — the only thing preventing double-delivery at the `prev_batch`/timeline-batch token boundary — is never exercised, because the fake's `prev_batch` (`p${startIdx}`) paginates strictly older than the batch it returns.
failure: Deleting the line `if (skip.has(e.event_id)) continue;` leaves the suite at 195 passed / 4 skipped. The `limited`-burst test in `catchup-sync.fake.test.ts` asserts `new Set(got).size === 5`, but with `syncCap:2` the fake's backfill chunk is `timeline[0..startIdx-1]` while `skip` holds `timeline[startIdx..len]` — disjoint by construction, so the guard can never fire. A real Synapse whose `prev_batch` is inclusive of the batch's oldest event would double-deliver that event as a `<channel>` push, and no test would notice the guard was gone.
remediation: Make the fake's `prev_batch` overlap by one event (the inclusive-boundary shape real homeservers exhibit), or add an explicit `prevBatchOverlap: number` knob and rows that set it to 1 and 2.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the burst test over `prevBatchOverlap in {0,1,2}` x `syncCap in {1,2,3}` x burst size, asserting delivered ids are exactly the burst, ascending, with no duplicate. Guards the CLASS 'a de-duplication guard whose triggering condition the fake cannot construct'; the same overlap knob also finally grades `stopAfter` boundary matching.

summary: `MESSAGES_ONLY_FILTER` — the server-side filter every catch-up read depends on — is verified by nothing: the fake deliberately ignores `/messages?filter=`, and no test asserts the emitted query string.
failure: Changing the constant to `{"types":["m.room.member"]}` leaves the suite at 195 passed / 4 skipped. Against a real Synapse that filter makes `/messages` return only membership events, so `drainForward` collects zero messages while `chunk.length >= limit` still advances `nextCursor` past them: every catch-up returns an empty page and the persisted cursor skips real history, silently and permanently. The only thing that would catch it is `conformance.test.ts`, which `describe.skip`s itself when no homeserver answers — as it does locally, and as it did for this round's green baseline.
remediation: Assert the filter on the wire: record `/messages` URLs in the fake and pin `filter` per call site (present on the `drainForward`/`recentWindow` pair, absent on `backfill`/`timelineTip`). Separately give the fake an opt-in filter-honouring mode so the client-side type filtering still has an unfiltered row to grade.
testUpgrade: A table over the four `/messages` call sites x {filter expected, filter forbidden} asserting the exact decoded `filter` param, plus a `fake.honorFilter` axis on the recent-window and drain tables so both the filtered and unfiltered server behaviours are graded. Guards the CLASS 'a request parameter the fake ignores'; apply the same URL-pinning to `dir`, `limit` and `timeout`.

summary: `sanitizeAlias` — the fold that keeps a topic name legal as a Matrix alias localpart — has no test in this package, and core's `topic-name.test.ts` grades a hand-copied duplicate of the regex with nothing binding the copy to the original.
failure: Replacing `sanitizeAlias` with the identity function leaves the suite at 195 passed / 4 skipped: every topic used in `packages/bridge-matrix/test` (`ctx-payments`, `payments`, `topic-A`, `hostile`, ...) is already alias-legal, so `safeName` returns it unchanged either way. `packages/bridge-core/src/topic-name.test.ts:11` re-declares the regex with the comment 'byte-for-byte the plugins' own module-private regexes' — a copy that can silently drift. With the fold broken, a topic like `ops:prod` or `team/frontend` builds the alias `#parley_ops:prod:parley.local`, `createRoom` 400s, `lookupAlias` fails, and `post` throws `createRoom failed (400) and alias unresolved`.
remediation: Export the fold (or the whole `roomLocalpart`) and test it here against topics that actually need it, including the injectivity pair (`a/b` vs `a_b`) and the 255-byte alias ceiling; or have core's test import the real function from each plugin instead of restating it.
testUpgrade: A table of hostile topic names — space, `/`, `:`, `#`, `@`, unicode, 300 chars, and the `a/b` vs `a_b` collision pair — asserting the produced alias matches /^#[A-Za-z0-9._-]+:[^:]+$/, is <=255 bytes, and is injective across the pair. Guards the CLASS 'a per-backend name fold whose only test lives in another package as a copy'; the same table applies to every plugin's sanitizer.

summary: `reportSyncFailure`'s power-of-two throttle carries the claim 'Rate-limited to powers of two so a long outage cannot itself become the flood', but no test grades it — the throttle can be removed with the suite green.
failure: Deleting `if ((consecutiveFailures & (consecutiveFailures - 1)) !== 0) return;` leaves the suite at 195 passed / 4 skipped. `subscribe-resilience.fake.test.ts` only asserts `errors.mock.calls.length > 0` and that call 0 contains '/sync failed'. Against a permanently broken `/sync` (revoked token) the unthrottled version emits one stderr line per retry — during the first minute that is one line per 200ms/400ms/800ms/... retry, i.e. exactly the flood the comment promises not to produce, and an operator's log is the only signal a dead live path has.
remediation: Assert the cardinality, not just the presence: for N consecutive failures the number of stderr lines must be ~log2(N)+1, and the reported `consecutiveFailures` values must be exactly the powers of two.
testUpgrade: Extend the permanent-failure table with an assertion that the set of `consecutiveFailures` values appearing in stderr over an observation window is a subset of {1,2,4,8,16,...} and that line count <= log2(attempts)+1. Guards the CLASS 'a stated log-throttle with no cardinality assertion'.

summary: `shared_room` is the one mode where inbound, member-forgeable data chooses which topic/allowlist bucket a message lands in — including the reserved presence topic — yet `connect()` emits no warning for it, while the strictly lesser default-password risk does warn.
failure: `connect({homeserver_url, user, password:'s3cret-real-pw', shared_room:'parley_all'})` logs nothing at all: the only branch in `connect` that warns is the default-password check. The code's own note says this mode 'MUST NOT carry mutually-distrusting topics' and the README says 'Production leaves `shared_room` unset'; both are documentation only. An operator who copies the conformance fixture's config into production gets forged-tag topic injection and presence-roster spoofing with zero operator-visible signal — and the only enforcement that exists (`shipped-artifacts.test.ts` asserting `shared_room` is undefined in the shipped examples) grades files in this repo, not the operator's config.
remediation: Warn on stderr from `connect()` whenever `sharedLocalpart !== undefined`, naming the forgeable `app.parley.topic` tag and 'leave `shared_room` unset in production' — the same shape as the existing default-password warning. Keep it a warning rather than a load error so the fixture and rate-limited deployments still work.
testUpgrade: Extend `creds-warning.test.ts` into a table over risky config shapes {default password, `shared_room` set, `room_preset: public_chat`} x {set, unset}, asserting exactly one warning per active risk, that each names the key and the mitigation, and that a fully safe config warns zero times. Guards the CLASS 'a security posture that exists only in prose' across every knob that widens the trust boundary.

summary: When a room's join is re-driven while an earlier join for the same room is still in flight (reconnect, or the first post adopting its identity nick), joinOnce rejects the superseded entry — and that rejection is delivered to the ORIGINAL caller, whose operation is aborted even though the successor join is about to succeed.
failure: Reproduced with a fake whose MUC handshake takes one round trip: `plugin.subscribe(t, h)` issued, then 5 ms later `fake.emit('online')` twice (a reconnect) -> subscribe rejects with `MUC join superseded for t-probe-b@muc.parley.local` and `subscriptions` is left EMPTY. Same result when the trigger is the first `post` adopting `identity.handle` as the nick (switchNick clears `joined` for every room, including in-flight ones): `subscribe` rejects and `fetchRecent` rejects with the same message. Because startPushLoop (bridge-core/src/transport/push-loop.ts:47) rethrows anything that is not NoSuchTopicError, and stdio-bridge's attach tears down and rethrows, a reconnect that lands during startup subscribes makes the whole bridge process exit(1) instead of retrying a join the successor is already performing.
remediation: Make supersession transparent to the loser: have the superseded PendingJoin settle from the successor (e.g. `superseded?.resolveFrom(entry)` / chain it to `this.joined.get(room)`), or treat the supersede error as retryable in `doJoin` so `ensureJoinedRoom` re-awaits the current cache entry. Neither switchNick nor rejoinAfterReconnect should convert a re-drive into a caller-visible failure.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a table (seam call in flight) x (re-drive trigger): {subscribe, fetchRecent, post, blocking fetchRecent} x {reconnect `online`, first-post nick adoption, occupancy-loss re-join} against a fake whose join reply is delayed one round trip; assert every row resolves (subscription registered / page returned) and that the room ends up in `joined` exactly once. The existing reconnect-rejoin and membership-revalidation suites always pre-seed `joined` with an already-resolved promise, which is exactly the shape that cannot observe this.

summary: `isSelf` treats ANY presence carrying MUC status 110 as this connection's own, without checking that its resource is the nick the pending join was sent for, so a join completes while the plugin's `this.nick` is not the nick it actually occupies — after which its own reflections fail the provenance check in onGroupchat.
failure: Reproduced: with `p.nick = 'nick-B'` and a join in flight for room R, feeding `<presence from='R/SOMEONE-ELSE'><x xmlns=muc#user><status code='110'/>` resolves the join ('resolved'). Downstream consequence reproduced in the concurrent-join probe: the join for the new nick is satisfied by the old nick's 110, the subsequent post is reflected from the nick the server actually holds, `resourceOf(from) === this.nick` is false, so the post is never correlated and hangs for the full POST_TIMEOUT_MS — observed `post rejected: post reflection timeout in t-race@muc.parley.local` after 15 s. The same shape occurs with no concurrency at all on a server that rewrites the nick (XEP-0045 status 210, 'service has assigned or modified the roomnick', used by nick-locking deployments): every post then times out at 15 s and every occupancy-loss presence for the real nick is only recognised via 110.
remediation: On a self-presence that completes a join, ADOPT the resource the server reported (`this.nick = resourceOf(from)`) rather than assuming the requested nick, and require either a resource match or 110-with-adoption before resolving; keep 110 as the self marker but never let it settle a join for a nick the presence does not name.
testUpgrade: Table-drive the join-completion presence: rows = {resource equals requested nick, resource differs + 110 (server-assigned nick, status 210), resource differs + no 110, resource equals a stale previous nick + 110} x {then post}. Assert the join settles only for a presence the plugin can attribute, that `this.nick` afterwards equals the resource the server used, and that the following post's reflection resolves within one round trip rather than at the reflection timeout.

summary: Two recovery branches the README advertises as safety properties are covered by nothing: mutating them leaves all 669 passing tests of the package suite green.
failure: Mutation 1: `const JOIN_RETRIES = 8` -> `0` (no cold-creation retry at all, so the README's 'joiners retry the transient condition, so concurrent cold-start is safe' becomes false). Mutation 2: delete switchNick's conflict fallback (`if (results.every(...)) return;` -> unconditional return, so the nick revert, the loud error and the re-join under the previous nick all disappear). Both applied together: `npx vitest run packages/bridge-xmpp` -> 'Tests 669 passed | 15 skipped', zero failures. The live conformance context even documents that it arranges the room in advance so 'the writers then never hit the cold-creation race', so no suite anywhere drives either branch.
remediation: Add fake-driven cases for both: a join that answers `item-not-found` N times then self-presence (asserting the retry ladder and that N > JOIN_RETRIES surfaces the condition), and a nick switch whose re-joins fail with `conflict` after rooms are already entered (asserting the revert to the previous nick, the loud stderr line, and that posting continues).
testUpgrade: One parameterized 'first failure then recovery' table over (failure condition) x (call order): conditions {item-not-found, recipient-unavailable, remote-server-not-found, conflict, forbidden} x orders {post-first, subscribe-then-post, fetch-then-post}, asserting for each whether the plugin retries, reverts, or surfaces — so any constant or branch in the retry/revert ladder that is deleted flips a row. Guard the class by asserting the observable behaviour (presences sent, nick on the wire, stderr) rather than the constants.

summary: The plugin defaults to the plaintext `xmpp://` scheme and neither warns nor enforces encryption for a non-loopback service, while `@xmpp/client`'s STARTTLS is purely opportunistic and SASL PLAIN is registered — so the account password crosses the network in the clear whenever the peer does not advertise STARTTLS.
failure: `backend_config: { service: 'xmpp://xmpp.example.com:5222', username: 'parley', password: 'real-secret' }` connects with no diagnostic of any kind. node_modules/@xmpp/starttls/index.js upgrades only inside `streamFeatures.use('starttls', …)`, i.e. only if the server advertises the feature, and there is no plaintext guard on the SASL side (node_modules/@xmpp/client/index.js registers `plain` unconditionally); an on-path attacker who strips `<starttls/>` from the stream features receives the credentials in cleartext. The README's own Prosody snippet instructs `allow_unencrypted_plain_auth`. The sibling backend already implements exactly this guard (`[parley-zulip] SECURITY: site_url … is plaintext http:// to a non-loopback …`, packages/bridge-zulip/src/index.ts:228), so the theme is fixed in one backend and open here.
remediation: In `validateBackendConfig`/`connect`, parse `service`: warn loudly (same shape as the default-password warning) when the scheme is `xmpp://`/`ws://` and the host is not loopback, and document `xmpps://` in the README config block. Better still, refuse a plaintext scheme to a non-loopback host unless an explicit opt-in key is set.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a transport-safety table shared in shape with bridge-zulip's: (scheme) x (host class) = {xmpp://, xmpps://, ws://, wss://} x {127.0.0.1, ::1, localhost, remote-host} x {default password, real password}, asserting exactly which cells warn/refuse and that no cell is silent — so a new backend or a new scheme cannot slip through unguarded.

summary: The README promises that a nick already held by someone else means 'the plugin logs a loud error and keeps posting under its provisional nick'; on the ordinary post-first path it instead fails every post and every fetch on that topic forever, with no log at all.
failure: Reproduced: fake with `joinReply='error', joinErrorCondition='conflict'`, `connect({password})` (nick unset), then `post(t, 'ctx-payments', 'one')` -> rejects `MUC join error (conflict) for t-conflict@muc.parley.local`; `priv(plugin).nick` is now 'ctx-payments' (never reverted), `console.error` was never called, and a second post rejects identically. `switchNick` only reaches its documented fallback when `joined` is non-empty, i.e. only if a subscribe/fetchRecent ran first — the same misconfiguration therefore produces two different outcomes depending on call order.
remediation: Pick one behaviour and make it order-independent: either detect the conflict on the first join and fall back to the provisional nick with the loud error (matching the README), or delete the fallback and document a hard `conflict` failure. Either way surface the same diagnostic from both orderings.
testUpgrade: A single table (call order) x (nick outcome): orders {post first, subscribe then post, fetch then post} x outcomes {nick free, nick taken by another account} asserting one canonical result per outcome column — so an order-dependent asymmetry in nick adoption fails a row instead of hiding in the branch the suite never drives.

summary: `REJOIN_CEILING_MS` (30 s) can never bind, because the loss counter gives up at REJOIN_LIMIT=6 and the largest computed wait is 6.4 s — yet the README advertises the ceiling, and the give-up message asserts a window the losses need not have fallen inside.
failure: `wait = Math.min(REJOIN_CEILING_MS, REJOIN_BASE_MS * 2 ** (losses - 1))` with losses ∈ 1..6 (losses > 6 returns early) maxes at 200 * 2^5 = 6400 ms, so `Math.min` is dead and the constant is unreachable. README:'That re-entry is deferred and backs off (200 ms, doubling to a 30 s ceiling, with jitter)' describes behaviour the code cannot produce. Separately, six losses spaced 59 s apart (≈5 minutes of wall clock) still log `… ended (…) 7 times inside 60000 ms`, because the window is measured between consecutive losses, not over the run.
remediation: Drop `REJOIN_CEILING_MS` (and the README's ceiling sentence), or raise REJOIN_LIMIT so the ceiling is reachable; reword the give-up log to state the actual predicate ('7 consecutive losses, each within 60000 ms of the previous').
testUpgrade: Assert the backoff LADDER as data rather than a bound: a table of loss index -> [min,max] expected wait derived from the constants, plus a case that walks losses to the give-up point and asserts the largest observed gap; a ceiling that no row can reach then shows up as an unused row instead of as dead code.

summary: `blockMs` is a silent no-op when `since` is undefined, although the plugin declares `supportsBlockingFetch: true` to the conformance suite and core's tool advertises long-polling 'whether or not you passed `since`'.
failure: Reproduced: `fetchRecent({ topic: 't-noSince', limit: 10, blockMs: 1000 })` on an empty room returns after 2 ms with `messages: []` and `nextCursor: ""`, because the `blockMs > 0` branch sits inside `if (since !== undefined)`. Core's fetchRecentBlocking then has to spend a whole `pollIntervalMs` nap before the native path engages (bridge-core/src/engine/blocking-fetch.ts), and a caller using the plugin directly gets no blocking at all on the arm core's tool description promises.
remediation: Take the blocking path whenever the queried window came back empty, including the since-less arm — for `since === undefined` an empty last-page window is equivalent to `since === ''`, so it can reuse `blockingMam(topic, '', limit, blockMs)`.
testUpgrade: Widen the conformance blocking case (and the local long-poll table) over the since axis: {since given, since omitted, since = ''} x {empty topic, topic with history} x {blockMs 0, blockMs > 0}, asserting for every empty-window cell that the call held ≥ ~0.9*blockMs or returned the message that landed mid-wait — so a backend honouring blockMs on one arm only fails a row.

summary: `fetchRecent` (a read) joins the topic's room, which auto-CREATES it and then submits a config making it persistent — so with a `post_topics` pattern an agent can mint unbounded, never-reclaimed MUC rooms and archives on a shared server by reading topics that do not exist.
failure: `parley_fetch_recent { topic: 'handoff/<random>' }` with `post_topics: ['handoff/.*']` (bridge-core/src/allowlist.ts — patterns gate post AND fetch and are matched against arbitrary caller-supplied names up to MAX_MATCH_INPUT) -> ensureJoined -> doJoin creates the room -> status 201 -> configureRoom submits `muc#roomconfig_persistentroom=1`. Each distinct read leaves a persistent room plus MAM archive behind; nothing in this plugin ever destroys one, and the read returns an empty page so the caller has no signal that it just provisioned server state.
remediation: Do not create rooms from the read path: for `fetchRecent`/`subscribe`, join without creating where the server allows it (or treat `item-not-found` as the documented absent-topic arm and raise NoSuchTopicError), and reserve auto-creation + the persistent config submit for `post`. At minimum document the growth and give operators the `restrict_room_creation` guidance next to it.
testUpgrade: A seam-call x topic-existence table: {post, fetchRecent, subscribe} x {room exists, room absent} asserting which cells are allowed to create a room (observable as a status-201 handshake plus a `muc#owner` config submit in the fake's `sent` log) — so any future call path that starts creating durable backend objects on a read fails a row.

summary: Three suites hand-roll their own weaker `@xmpp/client` stand-ins next to the shared `FakeXmpp`, because FakeXmpp records `send()` stanzas but not IQs — so the files that need to assert on an outgoing query cannot use the fake that enforces the wire contract.
failure: `FakeXmpp.iqCaller.request` never appends to `sent`/`sentAt`, so empty-archive-catchup.test.ts re-implements a capturing client (answers EVERY iq with a MAM `<fin>`, including a disco probe), reconnect-rejoin.test.ts re-implements another (answers EVERY iq with a disco#info result advertising MAM, so a MAM query in that file would be 'answered' by a disco reply), and mam-provenance.test.ts inlines a third. None of them enforce XML well-formedness, occupancy, or reflection stamping, so a defect on those paths is invisible in exactly the files that assert on queries; backend-config/creds-warning add two more inline client mocks.
remediation: Record IQ stanzas in the shared fake (`sentIqs`/push into `sent`) and delete the three ad-hoc clients, so every suite drives the one stand-in that models the server's contract.
testUpgrade: Replace the per-file clients with one shared helper and parameterize the query assertions over it: a table of (query kind) x (expected RSM/namespace shape) = {since-less last page, since='' from beginning, real cursor, lag re-poll, disco probe} reading from `fake.sentIqs`, plus a self-test in fake-xmpp.ts asserting that an IQ carrying an illegal codepoint kills the stream — which is what makes the shared fake strictly stronger than each deleted copy.

summary: `readRecent` arms a 200ms `FETCH_IDLE_MS` timer that closes the JetStream pull, and it is armed BEFORE the first message can possibly arrive (nats.js `fetch()` returns as soon as the pull request is queued locally — node_modules/nats/lib/jetstream/consumer.js:654-658). On any link whose first-message latency exceeds 200ms the pull is closed having read nothing, `wentQuiet` swallows the resulting error, and the page returns empty with `nextCursor = startSeq - 1`, which equals the caller's `since`. Core's `catchUpTopic` then hits its `messages.length === 0 || nextCursor === since` brake, so catch-up is permanently deaf while `post` and `subscribe` keep working. The README advertises exactly the deployments this breaks (`creds_file` for NGS, TLS material, a remote cluster).
failure: fetchRecent({topic, since:'0'}) against a stream holding m1..m3 where per-message pull arrival is 250ms (WAN/NGS RTT) -> {messages: [], nextCursor: '0'} on every call, forever. Reproduced with a fake whose close() has nats.js `stop()` semantics: latency=50 -> 3 msgs; latency=250 -> 0 msgs, nextCursor=0; latency=600 -> 0 msgs; a 5-page drain loop yields [].
remediation: Do not let a pre-first-message quiet period end the page: arm the idle close only AFTER at least one message has been read (a wholly-hole window then costs one FETCH_EXPIRY_MS, which is the case the idle close was added for), and/or derive the idle budget from the observed round-trip instead of a constant. Separately, never return an empty page whose nextCursor makes no progress because the plugin itself closed the pull — retry to the pull's `expires` or surface the truncation.
testUpgrade: Add a `latencyMs` axis (0, 50, 250, 600) to the fake pull in packages/bridge-nats/test/fake-jetstream.ts and cross it with every row of the shape/position table in window.test.ts and the completeness table in cursor.test.ts, asserting (a) the page returns every message in the requested window and (b) no page is ever empty while the window demonstrably holds messages. window.test.ts today only bounds elapsed time from above (`elapsed < EXPIRY_MS/2`) — a ceiling on patience with no floor — so it cannot catch this class.

summary: The fake pull's `close()` cannot lose a message: the generator yields its entire `window` synchronously and only then awaits the `closed` promise, so closing a pull always delivers everything. nats.js's `PullConsumerMessagesImpl.stop()` (consumer.js:511) unsubscribes and ends the iterator, discarding anything not yet queued. Every test grading the idle-close / short-read path therefore grades semantics the driver does not have, and the fake also models zero transport latency. Mutation proof: `FETCH_IDLE_MS = 1` — i.e. "return only what arrived in the same tick" — leaves all 144 fake-backed tests in window/cursor/cursor-input/resource/long-poll green.
failure: Mutate packages/bridge-nats/src/index.ts:70 to `const FETCH_IDLE_MS = 1;` -> `Test Files 5 passed (5) / Tests 144 passed (144)`, while the shipped read path becomes empty-page-forever for any link slower than one event-loop tick.
remediation: Make the fake's `close()` stop iteration immediately (race each yield against the closed signal and return, delivering nothing further), and give it a per-message `latencyMs`. Both are required before any assertion about the idle close means anything.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a fake that cannot fail the way the driver fails": add a negative-control test pinning the fake's own contract — closing a pull mid-window must yield strictly fewer messages than the window holds — as packages/conformance now carries a negative control. Then keep the FETCH_IDLE_MS mutation as a table: idle budgets [1, 200] x latency [0, 250] must produce at least one failing cell.

summary: The since-less "recent window" is sized in SEQUENCE space (`tailWindow = max(firstSeq, lastSeq - limit + 1, 1)`) while `limit` is a COUNT. Because the range is not dense (the README says so), a topic whose top `limit` sequences are holes (deleted tail, `nats stream rm-msg`) returns an empty page plus a cursor above every message it failed to return. Core's cold start adopts that cursor, so the retained history is skipped permanently and `parley_fetch_recent` reports a topic with messages as quiet.
failure: Stream holding seqs 1..4 (m1..m4) with `last_seq = 12` (5..12 deleted): `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 2})` -> `{messages: [], nextCursor: '10'}` instead of ['m3','m4']. Reproduced against the shipped fake with `visibleTail: 12`.
remediation: Widen the start on a short read: if the page returned fewer than `limit` messages and `startSeq > firstSeq`, retry with an exponentially wider `opt_start_seq` floored at `firstSeq`, until `limit` messages are collected or `firstSeq` is reached. Never return an empty since-less page while `info.state.messages > 0`.
testUpgrade: In packages/bridge-nats/test/window.test.ts replace `expect(page.messages.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(pos.limit ?? 100)` for the `no since` rows with an expectation computed from the shape (`shape.seqs.slice(-min(limit, shape.seqs.length))`) so every sparse row — front, interior and TAIL holes, generated seeds included — can fail; today 0 messages passes that row, which is the defect. Mirror the same count-not-range assertion in the shared conformance suite's `a since-less fetch returns the NEWEST messages` test with a sparse-stream variant supplied by the backend context.

summary: The push loop treats its OWN client-side long-poll cap as proof the event queue is live (`if (capped) { queueProven = true; recovered(); }`). A server that accepts the poll and never answers it (black-holed /events: a dead middlebox, a hung tornado worker, a silently dropped socket) is therefore graded healthy forever, so the topic stays advertised as piggyback-able and every blocking `fetchRecent` parks its whole budget behind a subscription that can never wake it — the exact invariant the `waiters`/`healthy` bookkeeping is documented to guarantee (src/index.ts:177-185).
failure: boot(); post(topic,'old'); tail = fetchRecent(topic).nextCursor; subscribe(topic, noop); sleep(200); fake.hangRoute('GET /api/v1/events'); sleep(1200); then post 'late' at t+100 while calling fetchRecent({topic, since: tail, blockMs: 4000}). Observed: returns at 4007ms (the full budget) with ['late'], and 0 dedicated queues opened (extra POST /api/v1/register == 0). Expected: a wake within ~PROMPT_MS, or a degrade to a dedicated queue. Via the MCP tool this is a `parley_fetch_recent` that holds for the whole `catchup.block_max_ms` (60s default) and then answers with a message that landed one second in.
remediation: Do not let an abort the plugin itself issued stand in for a server response. Require positive evidence of liveness: only set `queueProven`/`recovered()` when the queue has answered a poll with a parsed body (a heartbeat counts, a cap does not). Track consecutive capped-with-no-body cycles and, past a small threshold, `degrade()` and enter the same escalating backoff as a transport failure — a queue that has produced no bytes across N full caps is not a queue that is delivering.
testUpgrade: Add a 'the loop's /events is a black hole' row to the existing LOOP_STATES table in test/blocking-fetch.test.ts (prepare: subscribe, then `fake.hangRoute('GET /api/v1/events')`, then sleep past 2× events_timeout_ms) with reusesTheLoopQueue: false — that table already asserts the whole class ('NONE of them silently costs the caller its whole budget') but every existing row injects a fault that ANSWERS (a status code or a GC), so no row can reach the capped branch. Widen it to cross each LOOP_STATE with {answers-with-an-error, answers-slowly, never-answers}, so a future health signal that again confuses 'we aborted' with 'the server is fine' fails here.

summary: Same root cause, independently observable: because a capped poll routes to `recovered()` instead of `backoff()`, a permanently black-holed /events produces ZERO `[parley-zulip]` stderr reports. `backoff`'s own doc states the property being violated — 'so that a permanently dead push path is neither hot nor silent' — and the whole PERMANENT_FAILURES table in test/operability.test.ts exists to enforce it, yet the one failure mode that never yields a status code slips through it.
failure: boot(); subscribe(topic, collect); sleep(200); fake.hangRoute('GET /api/v1/events'); sleep(1500) (>2 cycles at events_timeout_ms=500); post(topic,'never-pushed'); sleep(3000). Observed: delivered=[] , 10 /events requests issued and silently discarded, 0 console.error lines containing '[parley-zulip]'. An operator whose live push has been dead for hours has no signal at all; core's channel path just goes quiet.

Name the distinct reason (e.g. 'events long-poll produced no response within the cap') so the operator can tell a black hole from a 500.
testUpgrade: Add a PERMANENT_FAILURES row `{ name: 'the server accepts every /events poll and never answers it', counted: 'GET /api/v1/events', apply: (fake) => fake.hangRoute('GET /api/v1/events') }` in test/operability.test.ts. summary: `fetchMessages` breaks pagination on `edge === undefined`, i.e. whenever a full page yields no usable record. The adjacent comment claims the raw-count guard prevents exactly this ('so that dropping one unusable record cannot be mistaken for the end of history and silently truncate the window'), but the `edge === undefined` disjunct reintroduces it for a page where ALL records drop. The same break makes `gapFill` return `Number(cursor)` unchanged, so the loop sets `needsGapFillFrom = undefined` and declares a dead-queue gap CLOSED — permanently dropping every message behind a full unusable page from the push stream.
failure: post(topic,'usable'); fake.injectRaw({topic, fields:{ id: -1 }}); then: fetchRecent({topic, limit: 1}) → {messages: [], nextCursor: '0'} while fetchRecent({topic, limit: 2}) → ['usable']. A model calling `parley_fetch_recent` with `limit: 1` sees an empty topic and a cursor reset to '0'. Scaled to the push path: GAP_FILL_PAGE (500) unusable records in a dead window make `gapFill` report the gap closed at the old watermark, and every usable message after them is never delivered and never retried.
remediation: Terminate pagination on the RAW page count only. Advance the anchor from the raw records' ids rather than from the normalized `Message[]`: keep the largest/smallest usable raw `id` seen (or, when none is usable, the raw record's own id, coercing exactly as far as `anchor` needs) so a fully-dropped page still moves the anchor and the loop continues. `edge === undefined` should be a reason to keep going with a shifted anchor, not a reason to stop.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the untrusted-payload hazard table over `limit` — for each hazard shape of `id`, assert `fetchRecent({topic, limit})` for limit ∈ {1, 2, 100} still returns every usable message on the topic (the table currently uses only the default limit 100 against a one-record topic, so raw.length < page always and the break is unreachable). Separately add a GC-recovery row whose dead window is `GAP_FILL_PAGE` records injected via `injectRaw` with an unusable `id` followed by N usable ones, asserting all N are delivered — that guards the gap-fill half of the class, which no limit-based case can reach.

summary: `wireTopic` writes into `claimedWireTopics` on EVERY call — including `fetchRecent` and the internal gap-fill read — and the map is cleared only by `connect()`. So a single read of a case variant permanently claims the wire name, and the topic the operator actually configured then fails `post`/`subscribe`/`fetchRecent` for the life of the process with 'Rename one'. The claim registry is a first-writer-wins global keyed on untrusted-shaped input: `parley_fetch_recent`'s topic argument comes from the model and, when a `post_topics` pattern widens the allowlist, need not be a configured topic at all. The map is also unbounded, so a loop of distinct pattern-matching topic names grows it without limit.
failure: configured = 'tmp-a-x9k'; a model calls parley_fetch_recent({topic: 'TMP-A-X9K'}) (allowed by post_topics: ['tmp-.*'] … or simply any two callers disagreeing on case). Reproduced at the plugin: `await plugin.fetchRecent({ topic: asTopic('TMP-A-X9K') })` then `plugin.post(asTopic('tmp-a-x9k'), …)` rejects with 'Zulip topic collision: … Rename one.' — permanently, with no recovery short of a reconnect, and no action the model or the operator can take at runtime. A read is not a write; it should not be able to take a namespace hostage.
remediation: Separate detection from claiming. Either (a) key the map by wire name → Set of Parley topics and only fail the call whose own topic is not the canonical one, seeding the canonical claim from the configured topic set, or (b) claim only on the paths that create durable state (`post`/`subscribe`) and let a read of a colliding variant simply read the shared history it addresses. Whichever arm is chosen, evict on `disconnect` as well as `connect` and bound the map, so a caller-supplied topic name cannot grow it without limit.
testUpgrade: Extend the CASE_PAIRS table in test/server-constraints.test.ts with a `firstCallPath` dimension — {post, subscribe, fetchRecent} × {post, subscribe, fetchRecent} — asserting that whichever path touches a variant FIRST, the topic that is actually configured/posted-to remains usable, and that a read never disables a write. Add a row that calls fetchRecent on N distinct case variants and asserts the plugin's claim state stays bounded, so the unbounded-growth half of the class is covered too.

summary: `SERVER_CONSTRAINTS.requestFlagDefaults` documents `dont_block`'s server default as `'false'` and the comment above it asserts 'Each default is the WRONG value for this bridge' — but `'false'` (blocking) is precisely the value this bridge wants. The `dont_block` guard therefore cannot fail, and its paired 'the fake behaves differently on the server default' case does not test the default at all: it sends an explicit `dont_block: 'true'`, proving only that the fake honours an explicit opt-out. Two of the six cases in the file are counted as coverage for a flag nothing grades.
failure: Mutation: delete both `dont_block: 'false',` lines from src/index.ts (the push loop's poll and `pollForWake`). `npx vitest run packages/bridge-zulip/test/wire-format-flags.test.ts` → 6 passed, including 'dont_block: the plugin overrides the server default'. The suite reports the plugin as sending a flag it no longer sends.
remediation: Correct the comment (only `apply_markdown` and `include_anchor` have a hostile default; `dont_block`'s default is the desired value) and change what the row grades: assert the emitted query string directly for the flag whose default is already correct — the plugin must send `dont_block=false` explicitly so a future Zulip default flip cannot silently turn push into a spin — or drop the row and stop counting it.
testUpgrade: Make the FlagRow contract carry the emitted request, not just the observed behaviour: add a `sentBy: (pair) => Promise<Record<string,string>>` that captures the actual query/form the plugin sent (the long-poll-deadline test already proves a `fetchWithRetry` spy is available) and assert the explicit non-default value is present for EVERY row. Then add a table-level invariant: for each flag, either the fake's default differs from the bridge's value (behavioural row is meaningful) or the row must assert the wire value — so a flag whose default coincides with the wanted value cannot be silently unguarded.

summary: `isPlaintextRemote` decides whether the HTTP Basic credential is going over the network in the clear by string-matching the hostname against `/^127\./`. Any DNS name beginning `127.` is misread as loopback, so the plaintext-credential warning — the only signal an operator gets that the bot `email:api_key` is on the wire unencrypted on every request — is suppressed for a genuinely remote host.
failure: connect({ site_url: 'http://127.0.0.1.evil.com', email: 'bot@x', api_key: 'real-secret' }) emits NO warning. Verified: `new URL('http://127.0.0.1.evil.com').hostname === '127.0.0.1.evil.com'` and `/^127\./.test('127.0.0.1.evil.com') === true`. Real resolvable names of this shape exist (127.0.0.1.nip.io and friends), so this is reachable by a copy-pasted or attacker-supplied site_url, not only by a typo. The TRANSPORTS table in test/creds-warning.test.ts has no row of this shape, so nothing catches it.
remediation: Classify by parsed address, not by prefix: reject anything that is not a literal IP as non-loopback (a hostname other than exactly `localhost` is remote), and for literal IPv4 parse the four octets and test `octet[0] === 127`; for IPv6 compare the normalized address to `::1` (and treat `::ffff:127.0.0.0/8` as loopback if you want the mapped form). Anchor the full hostname rather than a prefix.
testUpgrade: Widen the TRANSPORTS table with a near-miss dimension rather than adding one row: for each loopback spelling, generate the adversarial variants that share its prefix or suffix — '127.0.0.1.evil.com', '127.0.0.1.example', 'localhost.evil.com', 'notlocalhost', '1270.0.0.1', 'http://[::ffff:7f00:1]' — and assert plaintextRemote is true for every non-literal-IP host. A property test over `new URL(...).hostname` (non-IP hostname ⇒ warned, unless exactly 'localhost') would also catch spellings not enumerated.

summary: The GC-recovery table crosses DEAD_WINDOWS × FAILURE_POINTS (4 × 5 = 20 cases, each with a 60s timeout and up to 1001 injected messages). At deadWindow = 3 the gap-fill issues exactly ONE history read, so every FAILURE_POINTS row except 'nothing' arms `failNextMessagesRead()` for a read that is never issued: 4 of the 5 cases at that window are behaviourally identical to 'nothing' and cannot independently fail, while still paying full setup cost. The table's stated purpose — 'a failure BETWEEN two delivered pages is the case that grades the per-page progress watermark' — is unreachable for that dimension value.
failure: Instrumented probe: subscribe, post 'before', `fake.expireQueues()`, inject 3 messages, count `GET /api/v1/messages` via setResponseHook until all 4 are delivered → 1 read. Therefore `failsAfter(1)`, `failsAfter(2)`, `failsAfter(3)` and `n % 2 === 1` all arm a failure that never fires; mutating the per-page progress watermark (`onProgress`) cannot be detected by any of the four, and they are counted as four passing cases.
remediation: Derive the failure points from the window rather than crossing them blindly: compute `pages = ceil(deadWindow / GAP_FILL_PAGE)` and only generate rows whose failure index is reachable (`<= pages`), asserting in the row body that the injected failure actually fired (e.g. `expect(fake.requestCount('GET /api/v1/messages')).toBeGreaterThan(readsAtInjection)`) so an unreachable precondition becomes a failure instead of a pass. That removes 4 near-copies and makes the remaining rows independently falsifiable.
testUpgrade: Guard the class, not the instance: give the table a shared 'the fault I injected was actually exercised' assertion, so any row whose precondition is unreachable for its crossed dimension fails loudly. Apply the same guard to the other cross-product tables in the package (LOOP_STATES × blockMs in blocking-fetch.test.ts, PARK_POINTS × TEARDOWNS in subscription-lifecycle.test.ts), which have the same shape and the same exposure to silently inert rows.

summary: `longPollDeadlineMs` is a named export of the package's only public entry point (`exports['.'] → dist/index.d.ts`), i.e. it ships to npm as public API, but nothing outside `src/index.ts` references it — not the tests, not another package. `GAP_FILL_PAGE` next to it at least documents why it is exported ('so a test's dead-window sizes stay derived from it') and has a real test consumer; this one has neither, so it is a published compatibility obligation acquired by accident.
failure: `grep -rn 'longPollDeadlineMs' --include=*.ts packages/ | grep -v 'src/index.ts:'` → no matches. A consumer reading the .d.ts sees a supported helper; a maintainer changing its signature now faces a semantic-release major/minor decision over a function with zero callers.
remediation: Drop the `export` keyword (it is used only internally at lines 472 and 665). If it is genuinely wanted as a test seam, give it a consumer in test/long-poll-deadline.test.ts — that file currently recomputes the same arithmetic from `DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` by hand, which is the drift this export was presumably meant to prevent.
testUpgrade: Add a package-level export-surface test (the pattern already exists for source hygiene in bridge-core): read `src/index.ts`, collect every named export, and assert each is either referenced from `test/` or listed in a small explicit ALLOWED_PUBLIC_API array with a one-line reason. That fails the day a future internal is exported without a consumer, across this package's whole surface rather than for this one symbol.

summary: `openGateway()` resolves the gateway URL outside the retried unit: a failure of `GET /gateway/bot` charges the dial budget and rethrows without ever calling `scheduleReconnect`, so on the production configuration (no `gateway_url` override) one transient 5xx/429/network blip at startup kills live push for the life of the process — while the stderr diagnostic tells the operator "the reconnect ladder is retrying".
failure: connect({token, api_url}) with no `gateway_url`; one injected `500` on `/gateway/bot`; then `subscribe(topic, handler)`. Reproduced: subscribe resolves, exactly 1 `/gateway/bot` request is ever made (still 1 after 4 s of real time), no reconnect timer exists, a subsequent `post` is never delivered to the handler (`got === []`), and stderr says `live push for topic "730000000000000001" is not up yet (Discord GET /gateway/bot → 500: …); the reconnect ladder is retrying`. The bridge stays up serving REST, so the symptom is exactly the permanently-idle bridge the plugin's own comments say the design prevents. Recovery only ever happens by luck, if some later caller re-enters `ensureGateway` (a `block_ms` long-poll).
remediation: Make URL resolution part of the retried unit: have the ladder carry a resolver rather than a fixed url (e.g. `scheduleReconnect(() => this.gatewayUrlOverride ?? this.resolveGatewayUrl(), epoch)`) and, in `openGateway`'s resolve-failure branch, call `scheduleReconnect(...)` instead of only `chargeDialAttempt()`. Re-resolving per attempt is also more correct — Discord's `GET /gateway/bot` url is not guaranteed stable across an outage. Until the diagnostic is true, do not claim the ladder is retrying.
testUpgrade: CLASS: any step on the dial path not covered by the reconnect ladder. Widen the existing `Discord gateway recovery, whenever the failure lands` table with a second dimension — HOW the dial fails — whose cells include `GET /gateway/bot` answering 500, 429 and a transport error, crossed with `gateway_url` configured vs resolved, keeping the table's two assertions per transient cell (the plugin re-dialed on its own within `dialCeiling(window)` AND live push resumed once the gateway healed). Assert the stderr line claims a retry only when a reconnect timer actually exists. The current `rest-contract` case `the gateway handshake diagnostic neutralizes …` touches this path but asserts only the diagnostic's text, never recovery.

summary: `connect()` bumps `sessionEpoch` and clears `live`, but tears nothing down: the previous socket, the `gatewayReady` memo, `subs` and `waiters` all survive. The surviving socket keeps dispatching, yet `gatewayLive()` is false forever, so native long-poll silently degrades to an immediate return for the rest of the process and the new `gateway_url`/`token` is never dialed.
failure: connect({gateway_url:'ws://old'}); subscribe → READY; connect({token:'t2', gateway_url:'ws://new'}); then subscribe(otherTopic) opens NO socket (still only `ws://old`, still the old token's session), and `fetchRecent({since, blockMs: 30_000})` returns in 0 ms with 0 waiters armed — the long-poll never waits again even though the socket is healthy. Reproduced.
remediation: Either make `connect()` reject when already connected (fail-fast; the seam never asks for re-entrancy), or make it perform the same teardown `disconnect()` does (close the socket, clear `heartbeats`, `reconnectTimer`, `gatewayReady`, `subs`, `waiters`, `me`) before installing the new config. The `sessionEpoch` comment already describes connect() as starting the NEXT session, so today the code contradicts its own stated model.
testUpgrade: CLASS: session state surviving a lifecycle transition. The `Discord session state does not leak across a connect/disconnect cycle` table is parameterized over what the first session was doing but hardcodes `disconnect()` between sessions — add a second dimension over the TRANSITION (`disconnect()+connect()` vs bare `connect()`) and keep every existing assertion (only the new url is dialed, exactly one open socket, the dead session's handler unreachable, the new session carries push, and a blocking fetch still arms a waiter).

summary: Both post-disconnect quiescence guards are uncovered: mutating `isStopped: () => this.stopped` to `() => false` in `http()` and deleting `if (this.stopped) return { messages: [], nextCursor: args.since }` in the blocking path leaves the entire 252-case discord suite green. The docstrings claim these stop retries "the moment we disconnect" and prevent a woken long-poll re-querying after teardown; nothing measures either.
failure: Both mutations applied together: `npx vitest run packages/bridge-discord` → 252 passed / 10 files. With them, a 429 backoff keeps hammering the API for up to net-util's 30 s after `disconnect()` (competing for the shared bot token's rate-limit budget) and a long-poll woken by `disconnect()`'s own `wakeWaiters()` issues a fresh REST request after teardown — neither observable to any assertion.
remediation: Keep the guards and add the missing cases: (a) inject a 429 with a long `retry_after`, call `post`, `disconnect()` mid-backoff, and assert the call rejects promptly and `fake.requestCount('/messages')` stops growing; (b) park a blocking `fetchRecent`, `disconnect()`, and assert no further `/messages` request is made after teardown.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a disconnect-quiescence guard whose deletion is invisible. Add one parameterized table over ENTRY POINT (`post`, `fetchRecent`, `fetchRecent(blockMs)`, `resolveIdentity`, `subscribe`) × WHERE THE CALL IS PARKED (in flight, in a 429 backoff, in a long-poll wait) asserting for every cell that the request count taken at `disconnect()` never grows afterwards and the call settles within a bound — which would also cover future guards nobody thought to test.

summary: The comment-hygiene lint exists to stop history narration creeping into source "one line at a time", but its four regexes only match phrasings nobody writes (`we chose`, `reviewer`, `BUG-12`). The shapes people actually write — `used to`, `previously`, `as before`, `for historical reasons`, `now that we` — all pass, and the package source already contains one: `src/index.ts:348`, `// No long-poll requested → the durable exclusive-since page, exactly as before.`
failure: Prepending `// This used to be a plain number; previously we packed it by hand, which was slower.` to `src/intents.ts` leaves comment-hygiene at 13/13 passed. Control: `// as discussed with the reviewer…` does fail, so the lint has a true positive — its net is simply narrower than the class it claims to guard, and narrower than the source it already lints.
remediation: Delete `exactly as before` from index.ts:348 (the phrase's only content is a comparison to a previous revision) and widen BANNED with the history/justification shapes: /\b(used to|previously|no longer|for historical reasons|note: we now|was measured at|before this change)\b/i. Treat the lint as a floor, not a ceiling — its docstring should not claim the class "cannot creep back in".
testUpgrade: CLASS: a guard whose predicate can never fire on real inputs. Give the lint a NEGATIVE CONTROL table: `[bannedShape, exampleComment]` rows fed through the same matcher and asserted to be REJECTED, so every pattern is proven live and adding a pattern means adding its example. Ratchet the same negative-control requirement onto the sibling packages' copies of this lint.

summary: The blocking `fetchRecent` wraps only `ensureGateway()` in `withDeadline(…, blockMs)`; the two REST queries inside the same call carry net-util's default 30 s per-call deadline (`http()` never passes `deadlineMs`). So the call the code explicitly promises to keep inside `blockMs` can overrun it by up to 60 s.
failure: `fetchRecent({topic, since, blockMs: 500})` with a live socket: the first `fetchSince` hits a 429 whose `retry_after` is 20 s → net-util waits it in full → the one plugin call returns after ~20.5 s, 40× the budget core sized for the client's tool timeout. Worse with blockMs=60000: the waiter fires at 59.9 s, then the post-wake `fetchSince` can add another 30 s. Traced: `http()` passes no `deadlineMs`, so DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS (30 000) applies, and nothing recomputes the remaining budget around either `fetchSince`.
remediation: Thread the remaining budget into the REST calls on the blocking path — pass `deadlineMs: Math.max(0, deadline - Date.now())` through `getMessages`/`http` for those two queries (net-util already refuses a stated 429 hint that cannot fit the deadline, which is the desired answer here), or wrap each `fetchSince` in the same `withDeadline` and fall back to the empty replayable page.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a call that overruns its own declared budget on a leg nobody bounded. Parameterize a table over WHICH LEG STALLS (gateway connect, first REST query, post-wake REST query) × HOW (429 with a long hint, slow response) and assert for every cell that `fetchRecent({blockMs: B})` settles within B plus a small slack. The existing `Discord gateway handshake never completes` table only covers the connect leg.

summary: `requirePushableChannel` throws a plain Error for a DM or a `50001 Missing Access` channel. Core's `startPushLoop` rethrows anything that is not `NoSuchTopicError`, so `createStdioBridge`'s attach fails and the whole bridge dies — including catch-up and `post` for the other, correctly configured topics. That is exactly the outcome the same file argues against three methods earlier, where it deliberately resolves on a transient gateway failure because "failing here would fail core's attach and take the REST half of the bridge down with it".
failure: topics: [guildA, guildB, aDmChannelId]. `subscribe(aDmChannelId)` throws `… is a DM (type 1) …`; push-loop.ts:48 rethrows it (not a NoSuchTopicError), stdio-bridge tears down and the process exits — guildA and guildB lose live push AND catch-up over one mis-mapped topic. Traced through packages/bridge-core/src/transport/push-loop.ts:45-52 and transport/stdio-bridge.ts:85-100.
remediation: Pick one policy and apply it to both halves: report the per-topic misconfiguration as a loud stderr diagnostic (the shape the transient-dial branch already uses) and leave the other topics live, or surface it through core as an explicit partial failure. Either way, roll back `this.subs.set(channelId, …)` when the check fails, so the dispatch registry does not hold a subscription whose `subscribe` rejected.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a per-topic failure whose blast radius is the whole bridge. Add a case driving the real entry point rather than the plugin method — an allowlist of three topics where exactly one is unpushable, parameterized over the reasons (DM, group DM, 50001, plus the transient gateway stall as a control) — asserting the surviving topics still receive push and still serve `fetchRecent`. The current `subscribe on a channel that can never deliver` table asserts only that `subscribe` rejects, which is silent about what that rejection costs.

summary: The gateway harness is restated per file instead of shared, though `test/ladder.ts` already exists as the package's shared test-util module: `reachReady` appears four times (long-poll.test.ts:47 and :304, gateway-reconnect.test.ts:40, and as `session` in gateway-budget.test.ts:262), `stubFetch` three times, and `HUGE_HB`/`HANDSHAKE`/`NO_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` in four files — with the same two-line "Keep this ahead of `await pending`…" comment copy-pasted verbatim three times.
failure: A change to the handshake dance (say `subscribe` gains a second REST call before READY) has to be found and fixed in four near-identical helpers; miss one and that suite hangs on `await pending` with no indication which copy is stale. The two `reachReady` copies inside long-poll.test.ts are byte-identical, so one of them cannot fail independently of the other.
remediation: Move `reachReady`, `stubFetch` and the shared constants into `test/ladder.ts` (or a `test/harness.ts` beside it) and import them; keep exactly one copy of the fake-timer ordering comment, at the definition.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a fixture restated per test file. Guard it by construction: have the shared harness export the only `reachReady`/`stubFetch`, and add a hygiene case (this package already lints its own source) asserting no `test/*.test.ts` declares a local `reachReady`/`stubFetch`/`HUGE_HB` — so the next gateway suite is forced through the shared harness instead of adding a fifth copy.

summary: When Socket Mode is unavailable — including the wholly legal reactive-only config with no `app_token` — `blockForMessage` parks the caller for its ENTIRE budget and only re-queries `conversations.history` after the deadline, so a message that is already durably in history is withheld for up to `catchup.block_max_ms` (60 s by default). The plugin reports `supportsBlockingFetch: true` unconditionally, so core's generic 250 ms poll fallback can never compensate: the plugin consumed the whole budget inside one call.
failure: Reproduced (probe test, since removed): `connect({api_url, bot_token})` with NO `app_token`; `fake.createChannel('C0NOAPP')`; a message is seeded at t=300 ms; `fetchRecentBlocking(plugin, {topic, since:'0'}, {blockMs:3000, pollIntervalMs:250})` returns the message at **elapsed 3033 ms** with only 2 `conversations.history` reads in the window. With the shipped default `block_max_ms: 60000` the same shape yields ~60 s delivery latency per message, silently, for as long as Socket Mode stays unreachable (no app token, Socket Mode toggled off in the Slack app, wss blocked by egress policy).
remediation: Decline the native block when it cannot be served: if `app_token === undefined`, return the first (empty) page immediately so core's generic long-poll fallback re-queries on `block_poll_interval_ms` — that is exactly what the seam's "blockMs is only a hint" clause exists for. When an app token IS configured but the handshake is failing, re-query history on the dial-cooldown ladder (500 ms → 5 s) instead of only at the deadline, and loosen the poll-storm ceiling in `blocking-fetch.test.ts` to allow one read per dial rung rather than forbidding intermediate reads outright.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a table over the WAYS the event source can be unavailable × the moment the message lands: rows `{no app_token, apps.connections.open ok:false, pre-hello-close, silent socket, ws URL refuses}` × `{lands at 10%, 50%, 90% of blockMs}`, asserting for every row that the call returns the message within `landing + slack` (never `~blockMs`) AND that per-method request counts stay O(wall clock). The existing 'poll storm bound' rows only assert the ceiling, which "do nothing until the deadline" satisfies perfectly — add the latency floor so a bound that is met by doing no work fails.

summary: `subscribe` registers a route and opens the shared socket without ever asking Slack whether the channel exists or is readable, so the seam's `NoSuchTopicError` has no producer on the live path. A typo'd `channel_map` entry, a channel the bot was never invited to, or a forgotten `message.channels` event subscription all produce a `subscribe` that resolves successfully and then delivers nothing, forever, with no log line — while `fetchRecent` on the SAME topic correctly reports absence. This is the class bridge-discord fixed in the previous round ("subscribe never checked reachability, so a channel that does not exist or cannot be read produced a silent no-op").
failure: Reproduced (probe test, since removed): with `C0TYPO` never created in the fake workspace, `await plugin.subscribe(asTopic('C0TYPO'), handler)` RESOLVES, while `plugin.fetchRecent({topic:'C0TYPO'})` on the same plugin rejects with `NoSuchTopicError`. The CLI then prints `bridge up … live_push=true` and no `<channel>` event ever arrives; core's push-loop branch that logs `topic … does not exist on the backend yet` is unreachable for Slack.
remediation: After the socket is established, probe the channel once (`conversations.history {channel, limit: 1}` — no new scope needed) and map `channel_not_found` / `not_in_channel` to `NoSuchTopicError` so core skips the topic and logs it, propagating anything else. Keep the socket creation ahead of the probe so the existing subscribe-then-post idiom still works.
testUpgrade: Add `subscribe` as a fourth op to the `absent-topic.test.ts` CODES × OPS table (`channel_not_found` → absent, `not_in_channel` → absent, `is_archived`/`invalid_auth`/`ratelimited` → plain Error), so every future absence code has to state its subscribe answer too. Add one live row proving the negative control: subscribe on a reachable channel must NOT reject and must still deliver.

summary: `post` puts `content` on the wire as `chat.postMessage {text}` with nothing escaped. Slack parses `text` for its own control markup, so relayed untrusted content containing `<!channel>`, `<!here>`, `<!everyone>` or `<@U…>` becomes a real workspace broadcast/mention rather than literal text — the amplification class bridge-discord closed with `allowed_mentions`. Slack's own guidance is that a sender MUST escape `&`, `<` and `>` in user-supplied text; the plugin escapes none of them, and the fake accepts any body, so nothing grades it.
failure: `post(topic, handle, '<!channel> ship it')` — content an inbound Matrix/Discord message or a prompt-injected agent turn can carry verbatim through Parley — is delivered by Slack as an @channel notification to every member of the mapped channel. Same path: `'<@U0BOSS> approved this'` renders as a genuine mention of that user. Nothing in the plugin or in `test/fake-slack.ts` refuses or neutralizes either.
remediation: Escape `&` → `&`, `<` → `<`, `>` → `>` in `content` inside `post` (paired with the decode in the sibling finding so the round trip stays exact), or at minimum strip/neutralize `<!here|channel|everyone>` broadcast markup with an explicit opt-in knob. Make the fake refuse a `chat.postMessage` whose `text` carries raw broadcast markup, so the guard cannot be removed silently.
testUpgrade: A parameterized amplification table over vendor control markup in POSTED content — `<!channel>`, `<!here>`, `<!everyone>`, `<!subteam^S0X>`, `<@U0BOSS>`, `<https://evil|click>`, a bare `&`/`<`/`>` — asserting the bytes the fake receives contain no un-escaped `<`/`&`, and a fake that rejects the body otherwise. Guard the CLASS as "no inbound-derived string reaches a vendor markup parser unescaped", so the next transport with its own markup (Zulip mention syntax, Matrix HTML) inherits the row shape.

summary: `FakeSlack.handleHttp` replies `not_authed` and returns BEFORE `this.requests.set(method, …)`, so any request without an `Authorization` header is invisible to `hits()`. Every rate-limit/storm ceiling in the suite is expressed as `fake.hits(method) <= bound`, so a storm of token-less calls scores zero — and the missing-`app_token` configuration is precisely where the `apps.connections.open` storm is most likely.
failure: Observed in the probe above: a 3 s blocked `fetchRecent` with no `app_token` dialled `apps.connections.open` repeatedly (each reaching the fake and being answered `not_authed`) while `fake.hits('apps.connections.open')` reported **0**. A regression that dropped the app token, or dialled before it was configured, would satisfy every existing storm ceiling with room to spare.
remediation: Count the request first, then apply the auth check, in `handleHttp` — the counter's documented meaning is already 'did it reach the wire?'. Additionally record unauthenticated hits separately and assert they are zero in the happy-path tests.
testUpgrade: Add a fixture self-test (the pattern `documented-scopes.test.ts` already uses for its extractors): drive `FakeSlack` with a request that carries no `Authorization` and assert `hits(method) === 1`. Then re-run the poll-storm rows with `app_token` omitted as an extra table column, so the bound is enforced in the un-authenticated configuration too.

summary: The 'ack FIRST, before any processing' discipline that `onEnvelope` and `envelope-robustness.test.ts` both make load-bearing is not actually graded. Moving the ack to AFTER `routeEnvelope` leaves 298 of 299 tests green; the single failure is the `disconnect`-envelope row, and it fails only because the fake mints an `envelope_id` for a `disconnect` envelope, which real Socket Mode does not do. So the surviving guard is an artefact of the fixture, not of the contract.
failure: Mutation applied to `onEnvelope` (ack block moved below the `routeEnvelope` try): `vitest run packages/bridge-slack` → `Tests 1 failed | 298 passed`, the failure being `envelope-robustness.test.ts:223` ('a `disconnect` envelope is acked before the socket is rotated out'). Every row of the DROPPED table, the throwing-handler row and the ack-discipline conformance case all stayed green.
remediation: Grade the ordering directly rather than the eventual outcome: record, in the fake, the wall-clock/sequence position of each ack relative to a marker the plugin's handler emits, and assert ack-before-handler. Register a handler that busy-blocks synchronously for N ms and assert the ack landed at the fake before the handler returned.
testUpgrade: One parameterized 'ack precedes processing' table over envelope kinds {surfaced message, dropped subtype, unrouted channel, throwing handler, slow (synchronously blocking) handler}, each asserting the fake saw the ack strictly before the handler's completion marker. Separately drop the `envelope_id` from the fake's `disconnect` envelope so no test depends on acking an envelope Slack does not ask to be acked.

summary: The 'Multiple concurrent sessions' section justifies 'give every session its own bot' with a consequence that is no longer true: "their presence heartbeats all arrive as the same `senderHandle`, the roster collapses them into one phantom peer advertising whichever beat landed last, and hand-off by handle then targets the wrong instance." Core's roster keys on the presence RECORD's self-reported `handle` (`emitterOf` in `bridge-core/src/engine/presence.ts`, with `senderHandle` only as a pre-v2 fallback) and scopes liveness per random per-process `instanceId` — precisely so bot-token backends do not collapse. The conformance case that claims to pin this warning only pins that `senderHandle` collapses, which is true but does not support the stated roster consequence.
failure: Two sessions sharing one `bot_token` with handles `ctx-payments` and `ctx-reviews`: both beats read back with `senderHandle === 'U0PARLEY'`, yet `computeRoster` produces TWO distinct entries with correct topics and per-instance liveness. An operator reading the README provisions a second Slack app to avoid a failure that does not occur.
remediation: Rewrite the paragraph around the consequences that DO survive: message attribution in agent context (every peer's posts read back as one bot id, so a human cannot tell which session spoke), and the ~10-connections-per-app-token Socket Mode quota. Drop the roster/hand-off claim, or downgrade it to the case where `presence.enabled` beats are absent.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing README-vs-code guards (`documented-scopes.test.ts` style) with a case that drives the actual mechanism the prose claims: post two presence beats through ONE plugin instance under two different handles, run `computeRoster`, and assert the roster has two entries — so any README sentence asserting collapse has an executable contradiction. Guard the class 'a README consequence about core behaviour must be executed, not narrated'.

summary: `mention_map` is configured as 'Slack user/usergroup id → Parley handle' and is applied when rewriting mention markup, but `senderOf` returns the raw `user`/`bot_id`, so the same configured id becomes a Parley handle inside `content` and stays an opaque `U…` id in `senderHandle`. One person therefore has two identities in agent context, and handle-shaped consumers (roster display, `filter` globs over handles, any 'who said this' reasoning) see the id.
failure: With `mention_map: {U0ALICE: 'alice'}`, a message from U0ALICE reading `hi <@U0ALICE>` surfaces as `{ senderHandle: 'U0ALICE', content: 'hi @alice', mentions: ['alice'] }`. A `parley_list_users`/handle-filter view of the same human shows `U0ALICE`, while the text shows `@alice`.
remediation: Resolve `senderOf`'s id through `mentionMap` before branding the handle (falling back to the id when unmapped), so one configured mapping governs both fields. Update the README `senderHandle` row to say the map applies.
testUpgrade: Parameterize one table over the two identity surfaces: for `{mapped user id, unmapped user id, bot_id only, no user and no bot_id}` assert BOTH `senderHandle` and `mentions` on the history path and the live path from the same row — so any future field carrying an id has to declare whether the map applies to it.

summary: The describe is titled 'every string the shape guard admits must normalize' and its first case asserts 'the generator only produces strings the shape guard would accept' — but it checks its own literal `/^\d+\.\d+$/`, not the exported `TS_RE` (`^\d{1,12}\.\d{1,12}$`). 60 of the 100 generated values (widths 13, 17, 40, 400) are in fact REJECTED by the real guard, so the stated claim is false and the self-check can never fail — the same paraphrase drift `fake-slack.ts` warns about for `compareTs` and solves by importing from src.
failure: `TS_WIDTHS` includes 13/17/40/400; `TS_RE.test('9'.repeat(13) + '.1')` is `false`, yet the case asserting the generator matches 'the shape guard' passes. Tighten or loosen `TS_RE` arbitrarily and this case stays green, while the surrounding rows quietly stop testing the admitted range they claim to cover.
remediation: Import `TS_RE` and assert against it, then split the generator explicitly into an ADMITTED set (asserted to normalize with a well-formed timestamp/cursor) and a REJECTED set (asserted to be dropped, never surfaced), so both arms are named and non-vacuous.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a test must not restate a guard it can import': assert `TS_RE.test(ts) === expectedAdmitted` per generated row, with a positive control at each boundary width (12 admitted / 13 rejected on both sides of the dot). A widened generator over random widths 1..500 then also covers widths nobody enumerated.

summary: `packages/bridge-slack/tsconfig.json` includes only `src/**/*`, and the package ships no `tsconfig.test.json`, so its ~2.5k lines of test code are never type-checked: CI runs `npm run build` (`tsc -b`, sources only) plus vitest, which transpiles without checking. The repo-contract test that grades test tsconfigs only asserts 'there is at least one, so this check is not vacuous' — satisfied by net-util and conformance — so this package's absence is invisible.
failure: A test-only type error (e.g. the `plugin as unknown as { reconnect(): Promise<void> }` spy cast in `connection-lifecycle.test.ts` going stale after a rename, or a wrong `FetchRecentArgs` field) produces no CI failure at build time; it either passes as `any` or fails at runtime with a message that does not name the type mismatch.
remediation: Add `packages/bridge-slack/tsconfig.test.json` following the net-util/conformance pattern (path alias `@sharptrick/parley-slack` → `./src/index.ts`, include `src` + `test`) and wire it into the CI typecheck step alongside the build.
testUpgrade: Strengthen the repo-contract check from 'at least one package has a test tsconfig' to 'every package that has a `test/` directory has one, and it aliases its own name to src' — a table over the package list, so the next plugin cannot ship untypechecked tests either.

summary: The store's dedup set IS the once-only guarantee, but it is trimmed by retention. Once a record is evicted its composite id leaves `seen`, so a redelivered copy — which Telegram serves for ~24h from any unacknowledged backlog — is admitted as a brand-new observation with a fresh sequence. The README's "dedup across `getUpdates` backlog replays" is therefore false whenever retention rolls past a message still inside Telegram's replay horizon.
failure: connect with `observed_retention_per_chat: 2`; inject message_id 1/2/3 into chat -1001111000 (evicting id 1), then redeliver id 1. Observed: the live subscriber receives `-1001111000:1` twice (cursor '1' and again cursor '4'); `fetchRecent({since:'3'})` returns `[['-1001111000:1','4','one'], ['-1001111000:5','5','sentinel']]` — the same backendMsgId at two different cursors, a stale message re-presented above the agent's cursor and out of observation order. Core cannot absorb it: SeenSet is a bounded in-memory LRU, so it does not survive a restart or a busy topic.
remediation: Keep dedup independent of retention. Cheapest sound fix: track a per-chat floor of the highest `message_id` ever observed (Telegram's message_id is monotonic per chat) and have `append` refuse any record at or below that floor whose id is not in `seen`; persist the floor alongside the records. Alternatively keep a separate bounded ring of evicted composite ids, sized independently of `maxPerChat`. Either way a record refused for this reason must stay silent (it is a genuine duplicate), not reported.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing 'telegram observes each message once' ROUTE table over a second axis — retention state at replay time: `retention: [default, 2, 1]` x `route: [same session, cold restart, own post]` — so every route is graded once with the record still retained and once with it already evicted. Widen store.test.ts's DEDUP_CASES with a row that appends past `maxPerChat` and then re-appends the evicted id, asserting `append` returns undefined and `size()`/lineCount are unchanged. Every current dedup test uses maxPerChat >= 10, which is why the class is invisible.
