summary: The observed-message store — the full plaintext of every message this bridge has seen, in every chat the bot is in — is created with default permissions: 0644 file inside a 0755 directory. Both sibling stores in this repo deliberately do the opposite: bridge-core's ReadStateStore uses `mkdirSync(..., {mode: 0o700})` + `writeFileSync(..., {mode: 0o600})` for mere cursors, and bridge-sqlite pre-creates at 0o600 and chmods to 0o700 with the stderr note "the message store must not be readable by other accounts". Telegram's store holds strictly more sensitive data than either, in the same state directory.
failure: `new ObservedStore('<dir>/nested/deep/store.jsonl', 2)` then append; `stat` reports file mode 644 and directory mode 755 under umask 022. Any co-tenant account on the host can read every observed message body, sender handle and chat id. The compaction path is a second hole: `openSync(`${path}.tmp`, 'w')` also defaults to 0666&~umask, and `renameSync` installs that mode over the target — so even a store tightened after creation is re-widened by the next compaction.
remediation: Pass explicit modes: `mkdirSync(dirname(path), {recursive: true, mode: 0o700})`, `openSync(path, 'a', 0o600)`, `openSync(tmp, 'w', 0o600)`. Follow bridge-sqlite's norm for a pre-existing file too — if `statSync(path).mode & 0o077` is non-zero, `chmodSync` it down and write one stderr line naming the change, so an operator upgrading an existing deployment is not left silently exposed.
testUpgrade: Table-drive a permissions case over every file this package creates and over every path that creates it: `{target: store file, tmp file, parent dir} x {fresh create, create after compaction, pre-existing 0666 file}`, asserting `mode & 0o077 === 0` in each cell. Guarding the create-plus-compact-plus-adopt axis is what stops the next write path (a sidecar index, a backup) from reintroducing it. No current test in the package stats a mode at all.

summary: `post` checks `stillServing` before `sendMessage` but never after it. When `disconnect()` lands while the send is in flight, the message reaches Telegram, `ingest` hits `store === undefined` and returns on the one drop path in the whole plugin that emits no diagnostic, and `post` resolves with a backendMsgId for a message no store will ever hold. Own posts never arrive via `getUpdates`, so unlike an inbound message this one cannot be recovered on reconnect — it is permanently invisible to `fetchRecent`.
failure: Hold `sendMessage` on the fake, call `post(topic, SENDER, 'lost?')`, `disconnect()`, release. `post` resolves `-1002222000:2`; the fake shows the body was received; the store file contains only the earlier 'seed' record; stderr is empty; reconnecting a fresh plugin on the same store_path and calling `fetchRecent` returns `['seed']`. Contrast the adjacent behaviour the suite does pin: a post that races disconnect *before* the send is rejected and asserted never to have reached Telegram — so the plugin is strict on the recoverable half of the window and silent on the unrecoverable half.
remediation: After the `sendMessage` await, re-assert `stillServing(store)`; if the connection was torn down, reject with an error naming the sent-but-unrecorded `<chat>:<mid>` so the caller knows the message exists upstream and is missing locally. Independently, make `ingest`'s `store === undefined` early return report (throttled, e.g. `throttleAs: 'ingest-after-teardown'`) — it is currently the only unreported drop in a class where every other reason is named.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing 'rejects when disconnect lands mid-call' table with a second column for WHERE in the call the teardown lands: `{before the network call, after the network call resolves}` x `{post, fetchRecent, subscribe, resolveIdentity}`, using `holdMethod` to place it. Each cell must assert both the call's outcome and that nothing was accepted upstream without a local record or a diagnostic. The current row only ever lands teardown inside topic resolution, which is why the post-send half of the window is uncovered.

summary: The case named 'a post landing %ims into a blocking fetch is not missed' asserts only that the message eventually appears and that the cursor advanced. It never asserts the call woke on the message rather than on the budget, so the exact mutation it exists to catch — a gap between the initial query and arming the waiter — keeps it green. That is the lost-wakeup shape the review protocol names as this repo's richest vein, and no test in bridge-telegram covers it either.
failure: Inserting `await delay(5)` between `let messages = query()` and `await this.waitForMessage(...)` in fetchRecent reopens the gap: the post lands before the waiter exists, the waiter times out at the full blockMs, and the post-timeout re-query finds the message. All four cases (0/1/2/3ms) still pass; runtime goes from 128ms total to 5052ms EACH — a 160x latency regression on the plugin's advertised native long-poll, certified as conformant.
remediation: Add a wall-clock assertion to the race case: `expect(Date.now() - started).toBeLessThan(Math.min(blockMs / 2, 1000))` when `supportsBlockingFetch` is true, so a call that returns the right page at the wrong time fails. The 'blockMs is honoured natively' case already has this assertion for the 50ms post; the 0-3ms rows — the only ones that exercise the gap — do not.
testUpgrade: Guard the class by making WOKE-ON-MESSAGE, not merely SAW-MESSAGE, the graded property everywhere a native blocking fetch is exercised: parameterize `{postAt: 0,1,2,3,50} x {blockMs: 500, 5000}` and assert in every cell that elapsed time is far below blockMs as well as that the page is right. Mirror it locally in packages/bridge-telegram/test/guarantees.test.ts (which already owns the timing-bound style for disconnect-unparks) so the plugin does not depend solely on the shared suite for its own headline latency claim.

summary: The decision to park is made on `messages.length === 0` — the length AFTER `limit` slicing — rather than on "nothing exists after `since`". A non-positive limit therefore always produces an empty page, so the call blocks for the whole `blockMs` and returns nothing even though messages above `since` are sitting in the store. The JSDoc states the intent as "ONLY when the exclusive `since` query came back empty", which is not what the condition tests.
failure: `fetchRecent({topic, since: '0', limit: 0, blockMs: 1500})` on a topic holding two messages: returns after 1501ms with `messages: []` and `nextCursor: '0'`. The plugin's own limit-normalization test treats `limit: 0` and `limit: -5` as legitimate seam inputs, so this is inside the contract the package documents; core's `parley_fetch_recent` happens to declare `limit` as `.positive()`, which is the only reason it is not reachable from a model today.
remediation: Gate the wait on the unsliced predicate — e.g. compute `hasNewer = all.some(r => r.seq > Number(args.since))` and park only when that is false — or normalize a non-positive limit to "no messages, return immediately" before the block branch. Either way the block must not be entered when the store already holds something the caller asked to be woken for.
testUpgrade: Cross the existing LIMITS table with the blocking branch: `it.each([0, 1, 2, -5, 1000, undefined])` x `{blockMs: undefined, 400}`, asserting for every cell that when messages exist above `since` the call returns in well under `blockMs`, and that when none exist it waits and returns a stable cursor. The current limit table never passes `blockMs`, and the blocking cases never vary `limit`, so no cell of the product is graded.

summary: The `if (generation !== this.generation) { store.close(); this.stillCurrent(generation); }` block after the store is constructed can never run: the last `stillCurrent` in the chat-resolution loop is followed only by synchronous statements (`cfg.store_path`, `new ObservedStore`), so no `disconnect` can interleave. lifecycle.test.ts's own case comment says as much — "there is no await between resolving the last chat and publishing the store" — which is exactly why the branch is dead. It reads as protection against a race a maintainer will then assume is handled.
failure: Replacing the branch body with `throw new Error('MUTANT: unreachable')` leaves all 103 cases in lifecycle.test.ts + protocol.test.ts green, including the five dedicated connect||connect / connect||disconnect race cells parked on both `getMe` and `getChat`.
remediation: Delete the branch. If a future refactor introduces an await between the last resolution and publishing the store, reinstate it there — the invariant worth keeping is "nothing awaits between the final `stillCurrent` and `this.store = store`", which the code shape already states.
testUpgrade: Guard the class rather than the line: add a case that parks connect on `getChat`, calls `disconnect()`, releases, and then asserts `openFdsFor(storePath) === 0` — i.e. no store is ever constructed-and-abandoned for a retired generation, whichever await it happens across. That property survives the refactor the dead branch was anticipating, and it fails on a real leak instead of on an unreachable line.

summary: The same connect-a-plugin-against-a-fake-with-a-tmpdir builder is restated in eight of the ten test files under three different names and two different shapes (`startRig` in inbound.test.ts and again, near-identically, in cursor-lifecycle.test.ts; `connected` in guarantees/rate-limit/docs; `startFake`+`storePath`+`connectTo` in protocol; inline in lifecycle and poll-status). The stderr-capture helper is spelled out five separate times, once as a named `captureStderr` and four times inline. A reviewer cannot tell which copy owns a behaviour, so the next variant gets a ninth.
failure: The cleanup contract already differs between copies (inbound/cursor-lifecycle push a combined `fake.close() + rmSync`; protocol pushes them as two separate entries; guarantees relies on afterEach for `restoreAllMocks`), so a fix to teardown ordering must be made eight times or it is made once and silently not applied. protocol.test.ts:116 shows the drift already costing something: `const plugin = new TelegramPlugin()` is created, never connected, and `await plugin.disconnect()` is asserted on nothing while the real assertion runs against a different instance created inside `connectTo`.
remediation: Extract one `test/rig.ts` exporting `startRig(config)` (fake + tmpdir + plugin + `restart()` + registered cleanup) and `captureStderr()`, and have every file import them; delete the dead unused-plugin lines the duplication is hiding. This is a merge, not a new test — the cases themselves are good and stay as they are.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing 'telegram test suite hygiene' lint (docs.test.ts) from duplicate case TITLES to duplicate SCAFFOLDING: fail when more than one `*.test.ts` in the directory declares a local function whose body contains both `plugin.connect(` and `mkdtempSync(`, or more than one that spies on `process.stderr.write`. That guards the class against the next helper somebody re-types, which a title-only lint cannot see.

summary: `defaultStorePath()` is never executed by any test — every connect in the package passes an explicit `store_path` — yet the README and the `store_path` JSDoc rest a load-bearing claim on it: "absolute by default, because a store file that goes missing invalidates every cursor issued from it", and "the same state directory core keeps its read-state in". Both claims are currently true (traced against core's engine/read-state.ts:100), but nothing would notice if either stopped being true.
failure: Changing the function to return a relative `'observed.jsonl'`, or to a base other than `XDG_STATE_HOME ?? ~/.local/state`, keeps the entire suite green. The production consequence is the one the docs single out as unrecoverable: relaunching the bridge from a different working directory starts a fresh sequence space underneath cursors an agent is still holding, and `fetchRecent` then rejects every one of them as "ahead of every message this store has observed".
remediation: Add a case that connects with `store_path` omitted and `XDG_STATE_HOME` pointed at a tmpdir, then asserts the file appears at `<tmp>/parley/telegram/observed.jsonl`, that `isAbsolute` holds, and that the same shape is produced with `XDG_STATE_HOME` unset (relative to `homedir()`).
testUpgrade: Table the default over the environment axis that decides it — `{XDG_STATE_HOME set, XDG_STATE_HOME unset/empty}` — and assert absoluteness plus the exact `parley/telegram/` suffix in both, so the class covers the next env-dependent default too. Pair it with the docs lint already in docs.test.ts by extracting the expected path from the README `store_path` row rather than hard-coding it, so the code and the shipped claim cannot drift apart in either direction.

summary: A duplicated `Retry-After` header is parsed as no hint at all, so the loop retries at the 500 ms default against a server that asked for 120 s — the exact escalation-into-a-ban path the module documents itself as preventing.
failure: A 429 carrying two `Retry-After: 120` headers (a CDN/gateway plus the origin, both setting it, or two identical HTTP-dates). `res.headers.get('retry-after')` returns `"120, 120"`; `Number('120, 120')` is `NaN`, `Date.parse('120, 120')` is `NaN`, so `retryAfterFromHeader` returns `undefined`, `hinted` is undefined and `wait = DEFAULT_BACKOFF_MS`. Reproduced through `fetchWithRetry` with `maxAttempts: 3`: waits performed = `[500, 500]` — 240× sooner than the server asked, twice. `HEADER_ROWS` in the test table has no duplicated-header row, so nothing goes red.
remediation: Parse each comma-separated field-value candidate and take the maximum usable one (`raw.split(',')` → try `Number` then `Date.parse` on each trimmed part, keep the largest positive result); return `undefined` only when no part yields a positive duration. While there, reject non-decimal `delay-seconds` spellings — `Number('0x1F4')` currently reads as 500 seconds and `Number('1e3')` as 1000 seconds, neither of which is RFC 9110 `delay-seconds`.
testUpgrade: Widen `HEADER_ROWS` from a single header value to a *list* of header values appended with `Headers.append`, and cross it with the existing `PARSERS` matrix: rows for one value, the same value twice, two different delay-seconds, two HTTP-dates, a delay-seconds plus a date, and a usable value next to an unparseable one. The invariant to assert is the one already stated in the file — every performed wait >= the largest positive duration any field-value states — which guards the whole class of "multi-valued / oddly-spelled Retry-After degrades silently to the default", not just the duplicate.

summary: `MAX_ERROR_BODY` is applied only after the entire untrusted response body has been read into memory, so a hostile or broken upstream can spend hundreds of megabytes of RSS and the whole `deadlineMs` producing a 2 KB error string.
failure: A local HTTP server returning `500` and streaming 300 × 1 MiB before `end()`. `buffered()` calls `await res.text()` with no size limit, then `errorBody` → `sanitizeBody` truncates to 2 048 chars. Measured in this worktree: error message length 2 070, peak RSS growth **343 MB**, wall clock **11.5 s** — inside the default 30 s deadline, so no bound fires. The same unbounded read happens on every 2xx too. The doc comment on `sanitizeBody` claims the truncation stops "a hostile backend [pushing] megabytes"; it only stops them reaching model context, not memory.
remediation: Read the body through a bounded reader instead of `res.text()`: pull chunks until `MAX_ERROR_BODY * 4` bytes are accumulated, then stop and mark the result truncated (the surplus is discarded anyway). For the success path, either expose a `maxBodyBytes` option with a sane default and fail with a labelled error past it, or document that `fetchWithRetry` buffers without limit and stop advertising `sanitizeBody` as the thing that bounds a hostile body.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing `error-envelope.test.ts` real-server table over a `bodyBytes` dimension (`0`, `1 KiB`, `4 MiB`, `64 MiB`) crossed with the existing statuses and body behaviours, asserting both the message bound AND a resource bound the class needs: peak `process.memoryUsage().rss` growth stays under a small multiple of `MAX_ERROR_BODY`, and elapsed time does not scale with `bodyBytes`. That catches "cap applied after buffering" for any future path that embeds a body, not just the 500 case.

summary: 7 of the 20 conformance clauses have no `BROKEN_VARIANTS` entry, so their assertions can be gutted with the whole conformance package — negative control included — staying green, while eleven backends keep being certified against the weakened clause.
failure: Mutation, run in this worktree: (1) in `a post landing %ims into a blocking fetch is not missed`, replace the polling arm's `expect([...first.messages, ...second.messages].map(m => m.content)).toEqual(['racer'])` with `expect(first.messages.length + second.messages.length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0)`; (2) in `topics are isolated on the live path too`, drop the four cross-topic assertions and keep only the `length >= 1` checks. Result: `npx vitest run packages/conformance` → **7 files / 219 tests passed**, negative control included. After that mutation a plugin whose live path ignores the topic filter, or that drops a message landing in the read/waiter window, is certified conformant. `mustFail` targets cover only 13 clauses; uncovered are: `the same content posted twice`, `since at the tail`, `post accepts inReplyTo`, `on the live path too`, `resolveIdentity answers`, `blocking fetch is not missed`, `multi-process writes` — the lost-wakeup race among them.
remediation: Add a broken variant per uncovered clause (a subscribe that ignores its topic argument and fans every message to every handler; a `fetchRecent` that drops a message whose cursor arrived within N ms of the read, i.e. parks "from now" instead of at `since`; a `post` that returns a constant id; a `resolveIdentity` echoing a fixed handle; a cursor that resets between writers). Then make the one-to-one-ness mechanical: assert in `negative-control.test.ts` that every entry of `CLAUSES` appears as some variant's `mustFail`, so a new clause cannot land without a control.
testUpgrade: Add a table-driven check `it.each(CLAUSES)('clause %s has a negative control', c => expect(BROKEN_VARIANTS.some(v => c.includes(v.mustFail) || v.mustFail.includes(c))).toBe(true))`. That guards the CLASS — any clause added later, in any costume, must ship with the plugin mutation that proves its assertion can fail — rather than the two instances I mutated.

summary: Every `subscribe` case posts through the same `ctx.plugin` that registered the handler, so a plugin whose live path merely echoes its own writes passes conformance in full — and that is precisely the case Parley exists for (a human posts in chat, an agent must receive it).
failure: Traced: the only `subscribe` call sites are lines 248, 318, 360-361 and 388, and each is followed by `ctx.plugin.post(...)`. `ConformanceContext` exposes no second connected client (`concurrentPost` drives independent writers but no case pairs it with a subscriber). `ReferencePlugin.post` invokes the handlers directly from `post`, which is exactly the loopback shape — it is certified conformant, and so would a real backend be that subscribes to nothing and just fans out its own writes. The suite's own comment at line 384 concedes the gap ("needs a second, independent client the context cannot hand out yet") and then certifies anyway. Concrete failing scenario: backend X's `subscribe` registers no server-side listener; `parley` grades it conformant; in production no inbound human message ever reaches the `<channel>` event.
remediation: Add a required `ConformanceContext` field — `secondClient(): Promise<BackendPlugin>` (or reuse the machinery behind `concurrentPost`) — and a clause "subscribe delivers a message written by an independent client": subscribe on client A, post via client B, assert the handler fires with matching `backendMsgId`/`cursor` and the correct `topic`. Make it required, per this package's own stated doctrine that an omitted capability silently deletes coverage. The same client also closes the acknowledged hole at line 384 (that `disconnect` really stopped the live path).
testUpgrade: Parameterize every live-path case over a `writer` dimension — `['same client', 'independent client']` — so the isolation, ordering, once-only, identity-agreement and post-subscribe-tail clauses are each graded on both, and add a `BROKEN_VARIANTS` entry whose `subscribe` only echoes local posts so the new clause has a control. That guards "live delivery graded only against a loopback writer" as a class, including any future case that reaches for `ctx.plugin.post` after subscribing.

summary: `nextCursor` is documented as "the cursor to persist and replay verbatim", and catch-up-on-start is the product's core convention, yet no case ever disconnects and reconnects — so a session-scoped cursor is certified as durable.
failure: Traced: `connect` is called once per test, inside the factory; `cleanup()` disconnects and the context is discarded. No case calls `connect` twice or replays a cursor obtained before a teardown. A plugin whose cursor is a per-connection offset (`String(inMemoryIndex)`, a consumer-group PEL position, an expiring sync token) passes all 20 clauses; after an MCP restart, `fetchRecent({ topic, since: '17' })` against a fresh connection either re-delivers the whole topic or returns nothing, and core cannot detect it because it never compares cursors. Nothing in the suite or in `BROKEN_VARIANTS` can go red.
remediation: Add a clause "a cursor survives a reconnect": post, capture `nextCursor`, `disconnect()`, obtain a fresh plugin from the factory against the same backing store, post again, and assert `fetchRecent({ since: <pre-teardown cursor> })` returns exactly the post-reconnect messages in order. This needs the factory to be able to hand out a second context bound to the same store, which is the same capability the independent-client gap needs.
testUpgrade: Table the reconnect over where the cursor was minted — `['from a since-less fetch', 'from a paged fetch', 'from a live message', 'at the tail with nothing new']` — plus a `BROKEN_VARIANTS` entry whose cursor namespace resets on `connect`. That guards "cursor validity is session-scoped" for any backend whose ordering key is a handle rather than a durable position.

summary: The npm `description` sells "one fetchWithRetry loop (429 / Retry-After / backoff clamp / deadline / error-body redaction)" and the README's "two bounds worth knowing" names `MAX_BACKOFF_MS`, but `fetchWithRetry` never clamps anything, and `clampBackoff`/`MAX_BACKOFF_MS` have zero consumers anywhere in the repo.
failure: Traced: `fetchWithRetry` computes `wait = hinted ?? DEFAULT_BACKOFF_MS` and never calls `clampBackoff` nor references `MAX_BACKOFF_MS`; the only backoff it "invents itself" is the 500 ms constant, which is below the 5 000 ms ceiling, so the README sentence "`MAX_BACKOFF_MS` clamps only a backoff the helper invented itself" describes a code path that cannot execute. `grep -rn 'clampBackoff\|MAX_BACKOFF_MS' packages/*/src` outside this package returns exactly one hit: a *comment* in `packages/bridge-zulip/src/index.ts:1020` asserting that "the shared default and the shared ceiling stay in `clampBackoff`" — which is false in both directions, since zulip never imports it and `fetchWithRetry` must not clamp a stated hint. A reader of the npm page concludes their self-chosen backoff is bounded by this loop; it is not.
remediation: Drop "backoff clamp" from the `description` and rewrite the README bound to say what is true (the helper's own fallback is the fixed `DEFAULT_BACKOFF_MS`; a stated wait is honoured in full and refused only by `deadlineMs`). Either delete `clampBackoff`/`MAX_BACKOFF_MS` as unused public API — they are a published semver commitment with no caller — or wire the backends that ship their own reconnect ladders to them, and fix the zulip comment in the same change.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing `the stated-wait rule the README documents is the one the code runs` block into a general "named constant is load-bearing" table: for each exported constant, assert either that `src/index.ts` references it outside its own declaration or that some workspace package imports it — and that any doc sentence naming it can be falsified by a run. That catches the class "docs and npm metadata advertise a mechanism no code path reaches" for the next constant as well.

summary: `it.each([1, 2, 4, 5, 6])('paging from a cursor with limit %i is lossless')` has three rows that are the same case, and omits the only remaining discriminating one.
failure: Traced: the case posts 5 messages and pages from `all[0].cursor`, i.e. 4 remaining. Limits 4, 5 and 6 all return those 4 in a single page and then terminate — identical control flow, so no plugin defect can fail one without failing the other two; each row costs a fresh `beforeEach` connection (and, for a network backend, a real connect/teardown) to discriminate nothing. Meanwhile limit 3 — the only *uneven* truncation, 3 then 1, where an off-by-one in a page-boundary cursor lives — is not a row at all: 1 and 2 both divide the remainder exactly.
remediation: Reduce to the shapes that differ and derive them from the volume instead of hard-coding: `[1, 2, 3, posted.length - 1, posted.length + 1]` over a named `posted` array — smallest page, exact division, uneven truncation, exactly the remainder, and larger than the remainder.
testUpgrade: Make the row generator a function of the message count (`limitsFor(n) = [1, 2, 3, n - 1, n, n + 1]`) and raise `posted` to 7 so exact-division and uneven-truncation are genuinely distinct rows. That guards the class "page-size table degenerates to one behaviour as the volume changes", which will recur the next time someone edits the message list.

summary: `credentialParts` inspects only the URL path, so a credential in userinfo or the query survives into an error message whenever the body echoes that fragment alone — and nothing enforces the README precondition that makes this safe.
failure: Reproduced: `fetchWithRetry('https://u:sEcReT@api.example.test/v1/x', …)` against a 404 whose body is `upstream said: u:sEcReT@api.example.test` yields `L → 404: upstream said: u:sEcReT@api.example.test`. Same for `?access_token=sEcReT` echoed as `access_token=sEcReT`. The byte-identical split misses it (the body is not the whole URL), `credentialParts` misses it (it splits `pathname` only) and the `scheme://` sweep misses it (no scheme). No shipped backend currently uses userinfo or a query token — I checked — so this is a latent trap rather than a live leak, but the guard is documented as covering "the credential-bearing parts" and there is no test or assertion that would notice the day a plugin starts using either.
remediation: Add `new URL(url).username`, `.password`, and each `searchParams` value with length > 1 to the `credentialParts` set — the parse is already being done, so this is free — and keep the README caveat only for a bare `host/path` with no scheme.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing `SPELLINGS × VECTORS` credential matrix with a `CREDENTIAL_LOCATIONS` dimension — path segment (today), userinfo, query value, fragment — each seeded with the same `SECRET-CANARY` and each echoed both whole and as the bare fragment. The class is "a credential in a URL component the redactor does not enumerate", and a location-indexed table catches the next component too.

summary: The interleaved reader's 60 s give-up deadline can never be reached: the harness kills the test at 20 s, so the carefully-worded diagnostic it exists to produce is dead code and a stuck reader reports a generic timeout instead.
failure: Traced: `giveUpAt = Date.now() + 60_000` with `vitest.config.ts` setting `testTimeout: 20_000`, and the negative-control child run passing `--testTimeout=20000`. A backend whose reader never drains fails at 20 s with vitest's generic "test timed out" and the message `the interleaved reader did not drain <topic>` — the one line that tells the operator which topic and which failure shape — is never emitted.
remediation: Derive the budget from the test's own timeout instead of restating a larger number (e.g. take a `budgetMs` well under 20 s, or read the timeout from the test context) so the loop always loses the race to its own diagnostic.
testUpgrade: Add a self-test in `suite-shape.test.ts` that extracts every numeric literal used as a wall-clock budget in `src/index.ts` (`giveUpAt`, `vi.waitFor` timeouts, `blockMs`) and asserts each is strictly below the configured `testTimeout`. That guards the class "an internal deadline the harness pre-empts", which recurs every time a case grows a new budget.

summary: A shared HTTP helper lives in the `bridge-*` directory namespace reserved for backend plugins, so every mechanical derivation over the backend set has to hard-code an exception for it.
failure: `packages/bridge-net-util` is not a `BackendPlugin` and implements no seam method, but sits in the directory namespace `DESIGN.md` reserves for plugins. The cost is visible: `packages/bridge-net-util/test/fetch-with-retry.test.ts:933` must filter `d.startsWith('bridge-') && d !== 'bridge-core' && d !== 'bridge-net-util'` to recover the real backend set, and any future "run the conformance suite against every bridge-*" derivation will silently include a package with no plugin to test, or need the same exception list. The npm name (`@sharptrick/parley-net-util`) already omits `bridge`, so the directory is the odd one out.
remediation: Rename the directory to `packages/net-util` (matching the published name and matching `packages/conformance`, which is also a non-backend and is not in the `bridge-*` namespace), updating `repository.directory`, the vitest alias derivation and the two hard-coded exclusions.
testUpgrade: Replace directory-prefix heuristics with a manifest-derived predicate — a package is a backend iff its `keywords` contain `backend` (or it declares a `parley.backend` field) — and add a repo-contract row asserting that every `bridge-*` directory satisfies that predicate and every backend lives in one. That guards the class "the backend set is inferred from a naming convention and needs a growing exception list" rather than this one directory.

summary: The push handler emits whatever `m.topic` the plugin hands it, with no allowlist or reserved-topic check. DESIGN §14 states the bridge only subscribes to an explicit list; core enforces that on the SUBSCRIBE call but not on delivery, so an over-delivering plugin turns into agent context.
failure: A plugin whose subscribe primitive is coarser than a topic (a NATS wildcard subject, a Matrix room carrying several logical topics, a Zulip stream) that yields a Message with topic 'ops-secret' (not in `topics`) — or with topic == presence.topic — is emitted as `<channel topic="ops-secret">` and lands in the session. The reserved-topic guard that DESIGN §14 says makes presence unspoofable covers only the tool surface (allow.assert), so a presence heartbeat reaching the handler would be rendered as a normal message, contradicting 'the presence topic is never subscribed and never enters catch-up / dedup ... heartbeats never surface as <channel> events'. I could not confirm a shipped plugin that over-delivers, so this is the seam being permissive rather than a live bug.
remediation: Drop (and console.error once) any pushed message whose `m.topic` is not in the explicit subscribe set or is the reserved presence topic — strictness is the virtue at a protocol seam, and it makes the DESIGN §14 claim structurally true instead of dependent on every plugin's care.
testUpgrade: Add an over-delivering-plugin dimension to push-loop.test.ts: a fake whose subscribe(topic, h) invokes h with messages carrying [the subscribed topic, a sibling topic not in `topics`, the reserved presence topic, a topic differing only by case/whitespace], asserting exactly one emit for the legitimate topic. Guards the class 'core trusts a plugin-supplied field that crosses into agent context' rather than one wildcard backend.

summary: computeRoster does `Math.max(...recs.map(r => r.at))`, where recs is one entry per distinct instanceId in the page. The page size is a request, not a guarantee — nonconformant.ts explicitly models 'a page LONGER than the requested limit' as a shape core's loops must survive — so the spread argument count is plugin-controlled.
failure: A plugin returning ~200k presence messages with distinct instanceIds for the same handle (limit 500 requested) makes the spread throw RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded (verified the threshold: Math.max(...Array.from({length:200000},(_,i)=>i)) throws on this Node). parley_list_users then fails with an internal error instead of a roster, and the same page is O(n) memory in byHandle first.
remediation: Reduce instead of spread (recs.reduce((m, r) => r.at > m ? r.at : m, -Infinity)) and cap the number of messages computeRoster will fold (slice the page to PRESENCE_FETCH_LIMIT at the call site), so a nonconformant page degrades rather than throws.
testUpgrade: Run computeRoster/filterReachable against the shared NONCONFORMANT_SHAPES table the paging loops already use, plus a row for 'a page far LONGER than the requested limit with all-distinct instanceIds', asserting it returns (bounded time, bounded output) rather than throwing. Presence is currently the only page-consuming site in core not exercised against those shapes.

summary: The /mcp route validates auth but never the Host or Origin header, and the installed SDK (1.29.0 StreamableHTTPServerTransport) exposes no DNS-rebinding option, so nothing in the stack does it. The app also ships an explicit `insecureNoAuth` loopback mode.
failure: A bridge started with insecureNoAuth on 127.0.0.1:PORT is reachable by a browser the operator visits via DNS rebinding (attacker domain re-resolved to 127.0.0.1): the request is same-origin post-rebind, so CORS preflight no longer protects the JSON POST, and the page can drive parley_post/parley_fetch_recent — write and read access to the bus. I did not build a rebinding harness, so this is reasoned from the missing check rather than reproduced.
remediation: Add an app-level middleware next to the existing security headers: reject requests whose Host is not in an allowed set (default: the configured public URL host plus 127.0.0.1/localhost) and whose Origin, when present, is not allowed. It is a few lines and it covers the OAuth consent routes too.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a request-header table over [Host: expected, Host: attacker.example, Host: 127.0.0.1:wrongport] x [no Origin, Origin: expected, Origin: https://evil.example] x [insecureNoAuth, protect] asserting 403 for every non-allowed Host/Origin cell and 200 only for the allowed ones — a class-level guard that also covers the /parley/consent and /authorize routes mounted via configureApp.

summary: verifyAccessToken returns the live AccessRecord object out of `this.access`, and `issue()` stores the caller's `scopes` ARRAY by reference into both the access and the refresh record; exchangeRefreshToken forwards `rec.scopes` unchanged, so every rotation generation shares one array. A consumer that mutates req.auth or authInfo.scopes permanently widens the stored grant, across rotations.
failure: Untriggered today (the reactive server never reads req.auth), so PLAUSIBLE: `const info = await provider.verifyAccessToken(t); info.scopes.push('admin');` then a later verifyAccessToken(t), or any rotation of that grant, reports the injected scope; the refresh narrowing check `scopes.every(s => rec.scopes.includes(s))` then accepts it too.
remediation: Return a fresh object from verifyAccessToken (`{ ...rec, scopes: [...rec.scopes] }`) and copy `scopes` into each record inside `issue()`.
testUpgrade: Add an immutability table over every method that hands internal state out — verifyAccessToken, exchangeAuthorizationCode, exchangeRefreshToken — asserting that mutating each mutable field of the returned value (arrays, URL objects) leaves a second read of the same credential, and a subsequent rotation, byte-identical. Guards the class 'a store hands out live references' for whatever field is added next.

summary: The `event_id` cursor branch is deliberately protected against an unresolvable cursor (404 -> `recentWindow`, explicitly 'so that a purged event does not brick startup'), but the `@parley-stream:` branch passes its token straight into `/messages?from=` with no `allowStatuses` and no fallback — so an unparseable token rejects `fetchRecent` and, via `buildBridge`'s awaited `catchUpAll`, bricks every subsequent restart until the read-state file is hand-edited.
failure: A read-state file holding `@parley-stream:<garbage>` (hand-edited, truncated write, or a token minted against a room that no longer exists after a `shared_room`/`server_name` change) makes `drainForward` issue `GET /messages?from=<garbage>&dir=f`; Synapse answers 400 M_INVALID_PARAM for a malformed pagination token, `http()` throws, and startup catch-up fails permanently — the exact failure the sibling branch was written to prevent. Not reproduced against a real homeserver (no Docker daemon available in this environment), and the fake cannot show it: `tokenPos('garbage')` yields NaN and `timeline.slice(NaN, NaN+limit)` silently pages from the beginning.
remediation: Give the stream branch the same degradation: mark 400 and 404 as expected on the first `/messages?from=<streamToken>` request and fall back to `recentWindow` when the token is rejected, so both cursor forms have one recovery story.
testUpgrade: A table over cursor FORM {event_id, @parley-stream:, legacy '', foreign-backend value} x server answer {ok, 400, 404} asserting `fetchRecent` resolves (degrading to the recent window) and `catchUpTopic` comes up rather than throwing. Add a fake knob that rejects an unrecognized pagination token with 400 instead of coercing it. Guards the CLASS 'two cursor forms with asymmetric error handling'.

summary: README and examples/multi-session/nats/code-agent-a.yaml both tell operators a `subject_prefix`/`stream_prefix` mismatch across configs "silently maps 'the same' topic to a different subject/stream, splitting history with no error". Traced through `ensureStream` (src/index.ts:509-536) that is not what happens: on an existing stream name it swallows only the name conflict and never reconciles `config.subjects`. A subject_prefix-only mismatch leaves the second instance publishing to a subject no stream captures (JetStream 503 no responders — which `isStreamMissing` then reads as "stream vanished" and retries once before rethrowing), and `consumers.add` with a filter subject outside the stream's interest is rejected outright. A stream_prefix-only mismatch makes `streams.add` fail with a subject-overlap error the swallow regex does not match, so it propagates raw. Either way the instance is dead, with an error naming neither field.
failure: Two configs on one cluster, both `stream_prefix: PARLEY_`, `subject_prefix: parley.` vs `p2.`: instance B's `post('deploys', ...)` rejects with `503 no responders` (after one pointless re-add/re-publish) and `fetchRecent` rejects on consumer creation; the operator, following the README, hunts for split history instead of a broken bridge.
remediation: Have `ensureStream` verify the existing stream's `config.subjects` contains this topic's subject and raise an error naming `subject_prefix`/`stream_prefix` and both subjects; correct the README and the multi-session example comments to describe the real symptom.
testUpgrade: Add a table over the four prefix-divergence combinations (subject only, stream only, both, neither) driving two plugins at one cluster and asserting the class "a config divergence fails with an error naming the diverging field", parameterized so a fifth divergent field added later joins the table. A fake-backed row covers the same class by having `streams.info` report subjects that do not contain the plugin's subject.

summary: `validatePrefix` documents itself as rejecting an illegal prefix "at connect(), naming the field, rather than at the first post with a driver error that names neither", but its illegal set for `subject_prefix` is only `[*>\s]` plus control characters. `.` is unrestricted anywhere, so `"."`, `"parley.."` or any leading/duplicated dot produces a subject with an EMPTY token (`.deploys`, `parley..deploys`), which is not a legal NATS subject. connect() succeeds and the failure lands at the first `streams.add`/`publish` as exactly the anonymous driver error the function exists to prevent.
failure: `connect({ subject_prefix: '.' })` resolves; the first `post('deploys', ...)` fails on stream creation with an invalid-subject error mentioning neither `subject_prefix` nor the operator's value.
remediation: Validate shape, not just a character blacklist: require every dot-separated token of `subject_prefix` (ignoring the trailing separator) to be non-empty, and reject leading/consecutive separators at connect() naming the field. Same treatment for a `stream_prefix` that cannot begin a legal stream name.
testUpgrade: The prefix table in packages/bridge-nats/test/config.test.ts enumerates forbidden characters; widen it to a generated set over separator placement — `'.'`, `'..'`, `'.parley.'`, `'parley..'`, `''`, `'a.b.c.'` — and assert the class "connect() accepts a prefix iff the COMPOSED subject/stream name is legal" by composing the name and validating it, rather than by listing characters.

summary: `post` mints `backendMsgId` from an incarnation read in a SEPARATE round trip after the ack (`observeIncarnation`), so the sequence and the incarnation token are never observed together. Two reachable outcomes: (a) a stream re-provisioned between the ack and the info read labels the OLD incarnation's sequence S with the NEW incarnation, and the new stream's own message at sequence S later mints the identical id, so core's SeenSet drops a genuinely new message; (b) if the post-ack `streams.info` fails (the comment says "the cached incarnation is the best available"), the id is minted from the PREVIOUS incarnation's token — precisely the collision the incarnation prefix exists to prevent.
failure: Stream recreated out-of-band immediately after an ack for seq 6 -> post returns `<new>-6`; the new stream's real seq-6 message later reads back as `<new>-6`, `seen.firstSeen` returns false and core never surfaces it. Same outcome when the post-ack info read times out after an out-of-band recreation: post returns `<old>-1`, an id core already holds.
remediation: Observe the sequence and the incarnation in one consistent observation — compare `created` before and after the publish and treat a change as an unknown-incarnation ack, or confirm the acked sequence exists in the observed incarnation via `streams.getMessage(seq)` — and surface a distinct error rather than minting from a stale cached token when the observation fails.
testUpgrade: Extend the id-minter x observation table in packages/bridge-nats/test/msg-id.test.ts with two observation rows guarding the class "an id is never minted from an incarnation the plugin did not observe together with that sequence": (1) re-provision between `publish` resolving and `streams.info` resolving (swap inside the fake's info handler on its first call), and (2) `streams.info` throwing after the ack. Both must produce a disjoint id or reject; the current rows only re-provision between whole calls, which the post-ack read happens to cover.

summary: `post` rejects on `content.length > 2000`, i.e. UTF-16 code units, while Discord's 2000-character limit is measured in code points. Astral text (emoji, several CJK extension and historic scripts) is therefore falsely refused at half the real limit, and the error quotes a "characters" count that is not the number Discord counts.
failure: `post(topic, handle, '\u{1F642}'.repeat(1500))` → throws `Discord caps a message at 2000 characters; this post is 3000. Split it across posts…`, although the message is 1500 characters to Discord and would be accepted. The advice is wrong too: no split is needed.
remediation: Count code points — `[...content].length` — for both the check and the number in the message, and name the unit. Keep the direction safe (never under-count) if Discord's exact rule is in doubt, but stop refusing valid content.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a provider limit re-implemented locally in the wrong unit. Note the fake (`test/fake-discord.ts:203`) enforces the cap with the SAME `content.length` rule, so the `provider content limit` boundary table is self-confirming and can never see this. Make the fake count code points, then widen the SIZES table with a second dimension over ALPHABET (ascii, astral emoji, combining sequence, surrogate-heavy CJK) at limit-1 / limit / limit+1, so any unit mismatch between plugin and provider model shows up as a failing cell.

summary: `requirePushableChannel` refuses only channel types 1 (DM) and 3 (group DM). Every other id passes, including the ones an operator most plausibly mis-copies from Discord's UI — a category (4), forum (15), media (16), stage (13) or voice (2) channel — so the check that exists to prevent a permanently idle bridge admits several ids that can never carry a `MESSAGE_CREATE` for that topic. For a protocol seam, strictness is the virtue; a two-entry denylist is the lenient shape.
failure: `subscribe(asTopic('<a GUILD_CATEGORY id>'))` resolves with no diagnostic; the topic then never receives push, and the only signal is a later `post`/catch-up error from a different call site. No test covers any channel type other than 0, 1 and 3, so nothing pins the intent either way.
remediation: Invert it: accept only the types that carry guild messages under this intent set (0, 5, 10, 11, 12, and 2/13 if their text chat is intended) and refuse everything else naming the type and the reason, in the same message shape the DM branch already produces. That also makes a type Discord adds later fail loudly rather than silently idle.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a capability check written as a denylist over a provider enum. Replace the four hand-written UNREACHABLE rows with a table over Discord's FULL documented channel-type enum (0,1,2,3,4,5,10,11,12,13,14,15,16), each row declaring push-capable or not, asserting `subscribe` accepts exactly the capable ones and refuses the rest naming the channel id and type. A generator over `0..20` would also cover types nobody listed.

summary: The other half of the escaping pair is also missing: Slack returns message text with `&`, `<`, `>` HTML-escaped on both `conversations.history` and Socket Mode events, and `slackToMessage` passes it to `content` verbatim. So content is not what was posted, and each Parley hop that reads-then-reposts compounds the escaping. The in-process fake echoes `text` byte-for-byte, so the conformance clause 'post either round-trips %s exactly or refuses it' is graded against a server strictly more faithful than Slack.
failure: On real Slack: `post(t, h, 'if a < b && c > d')` then `fetchRecent({topic:t})` yields `content === 'if a < b && c > d'` — the conformance round-trip clause fails, and an agent handing that snippet on re-posts it, producing `&lt;` on the next read. Cannot be reproduced against `test/fake-slack.ts`, which never escapes.
remediation: Decode exactly Slack's three entities (`&`, `<`, `>` — in that order, ampersand last on encode / first on decode) in `slackToMessage`, and encode them in `post`, so the pair is symmetric and one round trip is the identity. Then teach the fake to escape on write and hand back escaped text, so the pair is actually graded.

summary: `routeEnvelope` closes the socket immediately on ANY `disconnect` envelope without reading `reason`. Slack sends `reason: "warning"` roughly 10 s ahead of a routine refresh precisely so a client can establish the replacement connection FIRST and drain the old one; closing on the warning converts a zero-gap rotation into a dial-round-trip gap on every refresh. Because `subscribe` restarts at the tail and core's push loop performs no periodic catch-up, messages in that gap never become `<channel>` events unless something independently calls `fetch_recent`.
failure: Slack pushes `{"type":"disconnect","reason":"warning"}`; the plugin closes at once, `close` fires, `reconnect()` dials `apps.connections.open` and completes a fresh handshake. Any `message.channels` event Slack delivers in that window is lost to the live path — invisible to a `live_push`-only session for the rest of its life. Not reproducible against the fake, whose `disconnect` row carries no `reason` semantics.
remediation: Branch on `reason`: on `warning`, open the replacement connection and only then close the old one (keeping single-owner rotation); on `refresh_requested`/`link_disabled`, keep today's immediate close. Model both reasons in the fake, including the overlap window where two sockets are briefly live.
